records.briefDescription: The single-edged, one-handed short sword built like an oversized knife, with its grip riveted through the tang and a Nagel on the cross to guard the hand; it is the weapon of Lecküchner's entire fencing system.
records.fullDescription: Hold the Messer in one hand and keep your empty hand on your back, bringing it to your chest only when you close for grappling or Messer-taking. The blade gives you a long (sharp) edge, a short (blunt) back edge, and a point; from the hilt to the middle of the blade is your strong, and from the middle to the point is your weak, so learn to feel where you stand in every bind. The Nagel projecting from the cross shields your hand and catches the opponent's blade. Come into the Zufechten without standing still to watch his strokes, for who displaces only will be hurt by the entire art. Set yourself in one of the four guards — Bastei low with the point on the ground, Luginsland high with the long edge forward, Stier with the hilt before your head, or Eber low on the right — or in the Schranckhut with the point down and one edge toward the man. Then step and strike as one action, turning the Messer in the bind so the long edge stands above and the short edge lies below, and drive your point long into his face. Everything rides on Vor, Nach, and Indes.
records.briefApplication: Use the Messer to seize the Vor in the Zufechten, striking bravely to the openings rather than waiting to parry, then working Indes in every bind.
records.fullApplication: Use the Messer to seize the Vor in the Zufechten, striking bravely to the openings rather than waiting to parry, then working Indes in every bind. Against an opponent set in a high guard like Luginsland or Stier, open with a master strike — the Zornhau to break strokes from above and shoot the Zornhau Ort to his face, the Wecker to break the Stier and Eber, or the Entrüsthau against everything struck downward from above. Meet his high threats with the long edge and thrust; answer a low attack by overrunning it with your longer reach. In the bind, feel whether he is soft or hard: if he presses hard on your strong, go high with the arm and Duplieren behind his blade with the short edge; if he is weak, Mutieren into a thrust to the lower opening. When he reaches for your blade, Durchwechseln beneath it to the far opening, or Zucken free of the bind and strike anew. Should he crowd in, bring your empty hand to his arm and go through into wrestling, pressing the hands or taking his Messer outright. Because the weapon is single-edged, keep turning the Nagel and short edge into play to shield your hand, and never merely displace — always follow the parry with your own work.

records.briefDescription: The Nagel ("guarding nail," or Werenagel) is a bar or ring projecting sideways from your Messer's cross toward the short-edge side, shielding your hand and giving you a hard surface to bind and shove his blade aside.
records.fullDescription: The Nagel is the defining fitting of the langes Messer: a heavy bar, sometimes formed as a ring, fixed to the cross and standing out sideways on the short-edge side, so it shields your hand where a thrust or a draw-cut sliding down his blade would otherwise reach it. Grip the Messer in a single right hand with the long (true) edge leading and the short edge to the rear; the cross and its Nagel sit as a broad transverse guard just above your fist. You do not strike with it — you bring it to bear by turning the hilt. In the bind, roll your hand and hilt across so the flat of the cross or the projecting Nagel beds against the flat of his Messer, then drive from the shoulder and step in to push his blade offline. Reaching toward the short-edge side, it catches his Messer where the bare cross would leave your hand thin, letting you trap and lever his blade or hilt while your point and long edge stay live to answer. Keep the arm structured behind it, so the shove comes from your whole frame and footwork rather than from wrist strength alone.
records.briefApplication: Reach for the Nagel when a foe is too strong in the bind: work with the cross or guarding nail to shove his Messer aside, then strike the Entrüsthau to the other peak.
records.fullApplication: Reach for the Nagel when a foe is too strong in the bind: work with the cross or guarding nail to shove his Messer aside, then strike the Entrüsthau to the other peak. Lecküchner names it in exactly this spot — when you strike the Entrüsthau with your strong and he displaces so hard that neither your Mutieren nor your Duplieren will come, stop matching strength edge-to-edge and instead lay the cross or Werenagel on his blade, push it offline, and cut the Entrüsthau to the other peak. This makes the Nagel your answer to a bind you cannot out-muscle: rather than surrendering the Indes to a stronger arm, you use the guard itself as a lever, borrowing the whole structure of the hilt instead of your edge. From that shove you flow into the close play the cross enables throughout the system — going with the hilt over his Messer, laying the cross to his elbow, or falling in to take his Messer outright in a disarm. Beware that committing hilt-forward carries you to grappling measure, where he can answer with Durchlaufen, wrestling, or a counter-grip; keep your point and long edge live so that the instant his blade is displaced you thrust or cut before he closes. Treat the Nagel as leverage and hand-protection, not a striking part — it wins the bind you would otherwise lose, then hands you back to the point, the long edge, and the winding.

records.briefDescription: The hooked butt-cap terminating the Messer's hilt, used as a blunt striking head against the ears, head, and chest and as a lever to go over the opponent's Messer or hand in close, armed-hand play.
records.fullDescription: To bring the Knauf to bear you shift into the armed hand: from a bind or a straight wind on his Messer, drop your left hand onto the middle of your own blade so you grip the Messer at both ends, turning the whole hilt—cross, Nagel, and pommel—into a short, powerful lever. Stand with the left foot forward, and as he commits his stroke, fall in with the armed hand, step your right foot well out to his right, and go high with the arm, driving the pommel down over his Messer or above his hand into his ear or head; the thumb turns above on the grip so that body rotation, not the wrist, delivers the blow. Keep the short point live throughout: once the pommel lands, twitch it back and set it at his chest or face, thrusting with the armed hand. Stepping your right foot well behind his, then your left foot behind him, lets you chain hilt-strikes to the head, stomach, and neck with your weight behind each blow, the point always threatening between them.
records.briefApplication: Reach for the Knauf once you are crowded in close in the armed hand, when the blades are too near to cut and you want to overwhelm him with blunt strikes and leverage.
records.fullApplication: Reach for the Knauf once you are crowded in close in the armed hand, when the blades are too near to cut and you want to overwhelm him with blunt strikes and leverage. Choose it out of a bind or a straight wind: as he strikes crooked to your left side or presses in too close for a clean edge, fall into the armed hand Indes, step offline, and answer with the pommel to his ear or chest rather than trying to out-cut him. It flows naturally from overrunning with the Entrüsthau—after you go from below over his Messer with the hilt and pull his blade back, raise the pommel and hammer his head, stomach, and neck as you step behind his forward foot. From the pommel strike, transition straight into taking his Messer: go with the hilt from above over his hand, or thread between his hilt and his hand and shove his Messer aside with your left elbow to strip it. If he displaces after the pommel lands, twitch the short striking point outside to his head and set your thrust anew. Against it, expect him to rush the Versetzen before your hilt arrives—grabbing your hilt behind your right hand with his left, striking your blade, and pushing you offline—or to catch your pommel-strike on a hanging point and wind with Mutieren against you in the bind.

records.briefDescription: The Messer's true, sharpened edge, lying on the same side as your knuckles when you grip the hilt naturally and opposite the short edge and Nagel; your strongest edge, leading your most powerful cuts and firmest binds.
records.fullDescription: Hold the Messer in a natural hammer grip and the long edge falls along the same side as your knuckles, directly opposite the short (false) edge, with the Nagel guarding your hand from that side. This is the true, sharpened edge, and it leads all your heaviest work. To bring it to bear from above, chamber high on your right shoulder or in the Luginsland with the arm stretched high and the long edge turned toward the man, then step in with the right foot and drive the cut down so the long edge bites first, the arm extending through the blow. In the bind you dominate by winding your Messer so the long edge stands above on his blade, thumb set on the flat for leverage; from that seat it carries your strongest pressure and threatens the point straight into his face. Because it sits toward the knuckles it also slices cleanly from below, running up into an arm or wrist. Whenever real force is wanted, the committed strike, the firm bind that stays strong on his Messer, or the pressing cut, it is the long edge that leads and the short edge that follows once you wind.
records.briefApplication: Lead with the long edge whenever you want maximum force: the committed strike, the strong bind that dominates his blade, or the powerful slicing cut.
records.fullApplication: Lead with the long edge whenever you want maximum force: the committed strike, the strong bind that dominates his blade, or the powerful slicing cut. It is your default answer to a stroke from above, an Oberhau; cut your own Zornhau so that as the Messers spark you wind the long edge above his blade, then shoot the point straight to his face in the Zornhau Ort. When you overrun a low attack (Überlaufen), strike long from the shoulder and remain with the long edge firmly on his Messer, then go high with the arm and hang the point in. Feel him in the bind: if he is hard, stay strong on the long edge, dominate above, and double behind his blade with Duplieren; if he is soft, shoot your point through or take the lower opening with Mutieren. Many master strikes open long and trade to the short: the Wecker and Geférhau strike with the long edge, then wind so the short edge finds the head, so treat the long edge as the powerful entry that buys you finer work Indes. Against a taking-away on the Messer, step offline and strike again with the long edge to the head, or turn your flat onto his and set the point. In the four cuts, run the long edge down onto his arms to press and slice. Its natural counter is a fencer who slips beneath your strength with Durchwechseln or Zucken rather than meeting it; feel that and do not chase the bind, but wind or set your point online instead.

records.briefDescription: The short edge is the Messer's false back edge, running opposite the long edge and often left flat or blunt except near the point, brought around by winding to strike over or behind the opponent's blade.
records.fullDescription: Because the Messer is single-edged, the long (true) edge runs along the front of the blade while the short edge sits on the back, frequently flat or blunt except near the tip where it is sharpened. You bring it into play by turning the hand and winding rather than by a fresh swing: as your point drops and your hilt rises high between you and him, bend your wrist so the short edge falls onto his face, head, or arm and cuts through as it lands. Laying your thumb flat on the back of the blade steadies this and lets you drive the short edge firmly through the windings and hangings. After a Wecker you angle the short edge out and strike short to his head, and from the Schranckhut you turn the long edge onto his Messer and then roll the short edge over onto his head. In the bind you can strike behind the blade of his Messer with the short (blunt) edge, doubling against his strong while your arm stays high and your long edge holds the bind, or wind so the short edge comes below and thrust to the face.
records.briefApplication: Choose the short edge when your long edge is bound or blocked and you need to reach over or behind his Messer to strike the head, face, or arm.
records.fullApplication: Choose the short edge when your long edge is bound or blocked and you need to reach over or behind his Messer to strike the head, face, or arm. It is the working edge of the winding game: turn your hand in the bind so the short edge touches his blade, let the point drop, and cut it across his face; after the Wecker, angle it out and strike short to his head; in the Wincker, strike long with the long edge, then wind and let the short edge fall behind his blade to the head in a doubled manner. When he displaces high and hard, do not fight his strong head-on but go high with the arm, stay on the blade, and strike the short edge behind his Messer as Duplieren. The Zwinger drives the blunt edge long from a stretched arm over his Messer into his face, and if he changes through below you remain in the Langer Ort so he can do nothing. Because these strikes live in Indes and the windings, they flow out of the hangings into further thrusts, cuts, and the four Schnitte into his arms. Beware that a canny opponent winds his own point against your short-edge cut and thrusts to your face first; if he does, wind again against his Messer or change through to the next opening rather than forcing the short edge home.

records.briefDescription: The Ort is the thrusting tip of your Messer, the point you shoot, wind, and hang at the face and chest, and the decisive end behind the Zornhau Ort, the Langer Ort, and the winding thrusts (some render it "peak").
records.fullDescription: The Ort sits at the very end of your single-edged blade, and nearly every thrust in the system turns on how you carry it. To shoot a straight point, extend your arm long and drive the tip at the face or chest, keeping the Ort online so your opponent cannot reach you before he must deal with it. When you thrust from a bind, wind your Messer against his so the long edge stands above and the short edge below, then let the point run forward to the face; if he grows aware and covers, wind again to the other side, always keeping the long edge up. To hang the point, raise the hilt and let the Ort droop over or under his blade so the tip stays aimed at his chest while your hands ride high. From the Zornhau you turn the long edge above and shoot the Ort forward the instant your displacement lands; from the Bastei you strip off the upper strikes with the point and from the Luginsland the lower ones, shooting it long before any bind forms. Keep the thumb on the flat to steady the tip, and let the point, not the edge, do the finishing work.
records.briefApplication: Lead with the Ort whenever you want to threaten or finish: a long point held in the face forces your opponent to answer it and lets you seize the Vor.
records.fullApplication: Lead with the Ort whenever you want to threaten or finish: a long point held in the face forces your opponent to answer it and lets you seize the Vor. The master rates the long point above the master strikes as a defense, since the strokes cannot protect themselves against it, so extend it against a man who rushes the bind, and if he strikes to knock it aside, work Indes: let the point sink and change through (Durchwechseln) below his blade to thrust at the far opening. After a Zornhau, shoot the Ort to the face or chest and turn the long edge above; if he winds it off, wind again to the other side or fall into the hanging point at his chest and push him back. Against the Stier and the Eber, go with the ready long point to the face and fall with your rear foot well outside, since those guards cannot protect themselves against a straight point. Use the Ort to set on (Absetzen) to the nearest of the four openings the moment he commits, and carry it through the four cuts, finishing a slice by winding the point back into his face. The Ort is answered in kind: an opponent may strike your wrist as you thrust, lower his own long point to your chest to shove you back, or wind against your point and beat you to the face, so cover your extension and stay ready to change through or hang.

records.briefDescription: The strong (Stärke) is the half of your Messer's blade from the hilt to its middle, where leverage is greatest, used to command the bind, receive force, and push an opponent's blade aside.
records.fullDescription: Divide your Messer's blade in half: from the hilt to the middle lies the strong, and from the middle to the point lies the weak (Schwäche). Because the strong sits nearest your fist and the crosspiece, it carries the greatest leverage, so force met there is easily held, turned, and overpowered. Work it by keeping a firm grip and driving the strong forward as the blades meet, going high with the arm so that your strong lies over his Messer. Seek always to catch the opponent's weak with your strong: when your strong grasps his weak you command the bind and may wind, press, mutate, or thrust as you please. The long edge commonly leads as you bind and dominate from above, while the crosspiece and the Nagel back the strong to shield your hand and let you shove his Messer aside. Keep your point online and your body behind the blade, and feel through the strong whether he is soft or hard in the displacement, for that feeling tells you whether to press through or to yield and work elsewhere.
records.briefApplication: Bring your strong against the opponent's weak to win the bind, receive his cut without being overpowered, and set up winding, doubling, or pressing.
records.fullApplication: Bring your strong against the opponent's weak to win the bind, receive his cut without being overpowered, and set up winding, doubling, or pressing. The choice turns on Indes: as the blades meet, feel whether he is soft or hard, and read where you stand strong and where weak. When he is strong and hard in the bind, pressing your strong with his own strong, do not fight strength against strength forever; wind the hilt under your arm, go high with the arm, and double (Duplieren) behind his blade with the long or blunt edge to strike his head, for doubling is worked against the strong of his Messer. When instead he is soft and weak in the bind, mutate (Mutieren) against his weak, hanging your point over his Messer and thrusting to the lower opening. In the Entrüsthau you strike with your strong, then drive your strong onto his weak; once you grasp his weak you may mutate to the neck or double behind the blade. Should he prove too strong in the displacement, do not force it: back your strong with the crosspiece and the Nagel to shove his Messer aside, or leave his strong and work your weak to the next opening. Beware in turn the foe who catches your weak with his strong, or who changes through (Durchwechseln) beneath your blade before you can settle the bind.

records.briefDescription: The Schwäche is the forward half of the Messer's blade, running from the middle down to the point — the section with the least leverage in a bind but the greatest reach and speed, where the point does its work.
records.fullDescription: Divide your Messer into two halves: from the hilt to the middle lies the Stärke, and from the middle down to the point lies the Schwäche. This forward half carries the least leverage against a crossed blade, so it cannot press or hold strongly, but it reaches farthest and moves fastest, and it is where the point lives. Whenever your Messer meets your opponent's, know at once which part is bound — if the blades cross near your point you stand in the weak, and you should not try to overpower him there. Instead keep the point online and let the weak feel through the bind whether he is soft or hard, then work Indes from what you sense. Extend the arm and the weak carries your thrusts and the Langer Ort into his face; turned edge-on, the same forward blade delivers the reaching cuts with the long edge. Because the weak yields under pressure, you answer a firm bind not by shoving with it but by winding, hanging the point, or changing through, letting your leverage travel back toward the strong while the weak still threatens with its point.
records.briefApplication: Read which part of your blade is in the bind and act on it — mutate against the weak of his Messer, and never overpower a hard bind while standing in your own weak.
records.fullApplication: Read which part of your blade is in the bind and act on it — mutate against the weak of his Messer, and never overpower a hard bind while standing in your own weak. The weak of the opponent's Messer is the target of Mutieren: when you strike strongly from your right shoulder and he displaces soft and weak in the Messer, wind onto his blade, go high with the arms, hang your point over his weak and thrust down to the lower opening. Duplieren is its partner against the other half — double behind his blade when you feel him strong, mutate over it when you feel him weak. Striking an Entrüsthau to his right side, turn your hand and wind the weak of your Messer over his, then finish with the long edge to his head. When you bind him firmly with the Wecker and feel him weak in the binding, wind through and take his neck, or if he answers strong work quickly with the weak to the next opening on the far side. Beware the mirror of this: commit your own weak against his strong and he can mutate or wind against you, so when he stands hard, hang the point, change through, or twitch off rather than pushing. In the grip and disarms the weak still serves — pull your hilt back so your weak rides onto his hand for Hände Drücken, and always fall to the weak of his Messer with the right hand when you go for the Messer-taking.

records.briefDescription: One of the four guards and the Messer's answer to the longsword's Vom Tag: left foot forward, the Messer held high before your head on a stretched arm, long edge toward the man, threatening descending strokes.
records.fullDescription: Set your left foot forward and extend the Messer arm fully so the weapon stands high in front of your head, hilt raised and the long (sharp) edge turned toward the man, the point angled up and forward. This is a high, open, extended guard, the functional analogue of Liechtenauer's Vom Tag, from which every stroke from above threatens. Because the arm is stretched rather than chambered on the shoulder, Luginsland reaches long: you can shoot the point straight at his face, fall into a powerful stroke from above, or launch the Geférhau by leaping in and cutting with the long edge from above while your arm stays high and the point sinks to his face or chest. The name means "look into the land," a watchtower stance: standing tall and stretched, you survey the four openings and wait, keeping your leg well in balance so that the man can make nothing whether he changes through or does what he likes. Keep the long edge leading and the point alive, ready to hang, wind, or let the point fall through to the other side.
records.briefApplication: Choose Luginsland when you want to own the high line and threaten descending strokes, forcing the man to answer your long, stretched point before you ever commit to a cut.
records.fullApplication: Choose Luginsland when you want to own the high line and threaten descending strokes, forcing the man to answer your long, stretched point before you ever commit to a cut. From here you seize the Vor: leap in with the right foot and strike the Geférhau, cutting from above with the long edge and letting the point drop to his face, or feint the cut and change through to thrust the far side. It is also a patient guard. Stand well balanced, hold the Messer stretched, and let him do what he wants; against strokes aimed at your lower openings you can defend with the point alone, stretching and shooting it from above at his face, and if you fail with the point, wind his Messer up into the Stier. Should he try to run in on you, go high with the arm and lower the point into his face or chest to push him off. You can also draw after from here: when he strikes long from his shoulder and his Messer sinks toward the ground, leap and strike into his opening before he recovers high. Beware, though, that Luginsland is the very guard the Entrüsthau is built to break; a foe who leaps offline and strikes the blunt edge to your upper peak will beat your descending stroke. So do not simply wait to be struck, but work Indes, hang and wind rather than trading blow for blow.

records.briefDescription: Stier (the Bull) is a high hanging guard: you hold the hilt up in front of your head with the point angled down at the opponent's face, like a bull lowering its horns — a functional counterpart to the longsword's Ochs.
records.fullDescription: To assume the Stier, set your left foot forward and raise the Messer so the hilt sits high in front of and to one side of your head, your hand turned so the short edge faces back toward you and the long edge stands outward. Let the point hang down and forward, menacing the opponent's face or throat from above — the lifted hilt and dropped point give the guard its name, a bull lowering its horns to gore. The Nagel and cross shield your hand where it rides high beside your head, and you keep the arm carried rather than rigid, the weak of the blade light so you can turn freely. Lecküchner forms the Stier from either side, and it doubles as the two upper hangings, so it is less a resting stance than a poised, point-forward threat you flow into and out of as the bind shifts. From here you can wind against an incoming stroke — meeting it with the short edge on one side or the long edge on the other — stay in the Stier, and thrust down into the face, or drop into the windings on both sides to hunt the openings above.
records.briefApplication: Take the Stier to hold the high line and threaten a descending thrust to the face, winding against strokes from above and answering them from your upper hangings.
records.fullApplication: Take the Stier to hold the high line and threaten a descending thrust to the face, winding against strokes from above and answering them from your upper hangings. Standing point-forward invites the opponent to commit; when he strikes down at your open side, wind Indes against his blade — short edge on one side, long edge on the other — staying in the Stier and shooting your point into his face from above, then remaining on his Messer to wind again to the far side if he sets the thrust aside. You can also flow into the Stier from another guard: when you stand in the Eber and he cuts high, go up and wind so the hilt rises before your head into the Stier, then step in and thrust to his face or chest. Against a foe who is himself in the Stier, do not merely displace — as he readies his thrust, come high with the long point in the Vor and drive it into his face, throat, or chest, for the long point beats the strokes on its own and they cannot protect against it. The Stier's own breaker is the Wecker: the opponent leaps offline and strikes his long edge onto your Messer, winding his point into your face. Guard against this by keeping your point online and threatening first, working Indes so his rousing cut finds a thrust already waiting rather than an idle high guard.

records.briefDescription: One of the four Messer guards: a low right-side stance with the hilt at your hip and the point angled up toward the opponent's face like a boar's tusk, the Messer's functional counterpart to the longsword's Pflug.
records.fullDescription: Assume the Eber most commonly on your right: set your left foot forward and hold the Messer down at your right leg with the hilt resting at your hip, so the blunt short edge is uppermost and the point runs forward and up toward the man's face. The hilt stays low while the point rides high, so the blade slopes upward like a boar's tusk driving from beneath — the Messer's answer to the longsword's Pflug. Keep the arm relaxed but the point true on his face or chest, poised to shoot a rising thrust the instant he commits. You may also take the Eber on the left: hold the Messer at your left hip with the long edge turned upward and the hilt sunk a little toward the ground, the point again standing up against his face. Either side rests in one of the two lower hangings, so your natural work from here is to wind through those hangings, each winding offering a stroke, a thrust, or a cut. Stay soft and coiled rather than braced; the guard's strength is the threat of the waiting point, not muscled tension in the arm.
records.briefApplication: Choose the Eber to bait and set aside an incoming thrust, then answer instantly with your own rising thrust to his face or chest.
records.fullApplication: Choose the Eber to bait and set aside an incoming thrust, then answer instantly with your own rising thrust to his face or chest. Standing on your right in the guard, expose your left opening as bait; when he thrusts, wind against him so your short edge catches his Messer and sets it aside (Absetzen) with your point already online, then drive the point home to the face or body. If instead he strikes down at your left side, go up with the Messer and wind so the hilt comes before your head — you arrive in the Stier — then step in and thrust to the face or chest. Because the Eber sits in the two lower hangings, you always keep the windings in reserve: feel his pressure Indes and turn a winding into whichever opening he leaves, taking the stroke, thrust, or cut as it offers. Be wary that a point-forward stance is itself vulnerable to the point. The Zwinger is the stroke the master sets against the Eber, and he rates the Langer Ort surer still — he meets your thrust with a long straight point to your face and drops his rear foot wide to reach past you. So threaten first and keep your own point live, forcing him to answer your Vor rather than settle the long point on you unopposed.

records.briefDescription: The first of Lecküchner's four guards: a low, provocative bulwark held with the left foot forward and the stretched Messer's point on the ground, short edge above — the functional analogue of the longsword's Alber.
records.fullDescription: Assume the Bastei by putting your left foot forward and holding the Messer in your stretched arm out in front of you, letting the point sink all the way to the ground so the short edge faces upward. The arm hangs long, the hilt low before your body, so the whole weapon slopes down and forward like a bulwark thrown across your line. Though the posture looks open and inviting, it is coiled: from the sunk point you can rise in a single motion, driving the point up beneath an incoming blade to his face or chest with the stretched arm, shooting the Langer Ort the master calls the best defense in the Messer. The guard roughly mirrors Liechtenauer's Alber (Fool) — it deliberately offers the openings to draw a committed attack, then answers upward with the point rather than parrying across. You may hold it on either side: with the left foot leading as described, or on the left side with the right foot forward, from which you can equally strike, thrust and cut, though the master warns it works a little worse and feels awkward until you are trained in it.
records.briefApplication: Choose the Bastei to bait an aggressive opponent into committing to your openings, then strip his blow aside with the point and thrust up into his face or chest.
records.fullApplication: Choose the Bastei to bait an aggressive opponent into committing to your openings, then strip his blow aside with the point and thrust up into his face or chest. It shines against fighters who rush in: hold the point forward and let him run onto it, and if he tries to displace it and reaches for your Messer, change through (Durchwechseln) Indes to the next opening. Whatever he aims at your upper peaks, defend with the Langer Ort — the best defense in the Messer — and if he tries to seize the Vor, take it from him on the point and work Indes according to the Nach. If your thrust lands and he flinches back, fall straight into the Bastei again and draw your rear foot back, never letting yourself be moved from the guard unharmed. When he binds high, go up with the point to his face; when he sinks low with the arm, close for the wrestling. Should he crook onto your blade or fall on it, change through below. Its natural counter comes from above: the Geférhau breaks the Bastei, and who aims at the Bastei is hurt from the Luginsland, whose high point answers your low one — so against a foe in that high guard, go up under his Messer, change through, and thrust, adding Duplieren or going through as he gives you the bind.

records.briefDescription: The barrier guard: a low, crossed stance in which you rest the Messer's point on the ground to one side, short edge toward the man and the arm barred across your body — a favored launch point for the master strikes.
records.fullDescription: Schrankhut comes in a right-side and a left-side form, and both set the leading foot opposite the side the point rests on — the crossing that gives the guard its name. For the left barrier, put your right foot forward and hold the Messer with its point down on the ground to your left, so the short (blunt) edge faces the man; for the right barrier, put your left foot forward and carry the point down to your right, again with the short edge toward him. Either way the arm bars low across your body while the Nagel and cross shield your hand and the point loiters near the earth. Deliberately expose the open side to invite a strike. From here you spring: leap or step well offline out of the incoming blow, wind the hilt up under your arm, and drive the long edge onto his Messer, then turn the short edge onto his head or thrust the point to his face. Because the point is already gathered low and the arm coiled, the barrier loads a Wecker, a changing-through, or a winding thrust with almost no warning.
records.briefApplication: Rest in the Schrankhut at the onset to bait an overhead strike, then spring offline and answer with the Wecker or a winding thrust to the face.
records.fullApplication: Rest in the Schrankhut at the onset to bait an overhead strike, then spring offline and answer with the Wecker or a winding thrust to the face. It is above all a launching platform: from the barrier you can throw the Wecker on either side to break his Stier or Eber. Expose your open flank, and when he commits a strike from above, leap from the stroke, drive the long edge onto his Messer, and Indes wind the point into his face. Against a man in the Luginsland or Stier, act as if you would strike the Wecker but do not deliver it — Indes change through to the next peak and thrust to his other side, much like the Geférhau's strike-into-changing-through. When the Messers spark together in the bind, wind the point to his face, strike the short edge onto his head, or cut skillfully from one peak to the other. The barrier also serves roughly against clumsy peasant strokes: keep the point aimed at his face and strike in as the blades clash, then sweep around his head to the neck. Beware a cool opponent who refuses the bind and holds a straight Langer Ort: he can spoil your changing-through, thrusting into your face as you cross under, so do not over-commit the cross and stay ready to wind against his openings if he stays hard.

records.briefDescription: The first master strike: a wrathful descending diagonal cut from your right shoulder, delivered with the long edge, that answers an overhead attack by striking into it to form a strong bind from which you work Indes.
records.fullDescription: Begin with the Messer chambered high on your right shoulder, left foot forward, or drawn up from the Schranckhut. As your opponent hews down at your head from his right, step in with your right foot and drive a wrathful diagonal cut from high right to low left, the long edge leading. Rather than parrying wide, strike angrily into his descending blade so both cuts meet above and you displace his stroke while landing your own, meeting force with force to form a strong bind. Keep the arm firm and let the point run forward: turn your Messer against his so the long edge stands above and the short edge below, shooting the Ort toward his face or chest. Your body unwinds from the hips behind the blow, the Nagel and hilt guarding your hand. From that bind you do not simply hold; through the crossed blades you feel whether he is soft or hard, and stay poised to wind, thrust, or take away Indes.
records.briefApplication: Choose the Zornhau as your primary answer whenever an opponent hews at you from above, meeting his Oberhau with a strike that both displaces and threatens at once.
records.fullApplication: Choose the Zornhau as your primary answer whenever an opponent hews at you from above, meeting his Oberhau with a strike that both displaces and threatens at once. Lecküchner calls it a simple peasant stroke, yet its point breaks all the strokes from above: the strength lies in seizing the Vor and turning his attack into your bind. Once bound, work Indes and feel whether he is soft or hard on your Messer. If he is soft and yields, shoot the Zornhau Ort straight to his face or chest with the long edge above. If he grows aware of the point and displaces, go high with the arm and wind the point over his blade to the face on his left, the war of windings; if he sets that aside, drop to the other peak under his arm to the chest. You may instead take away, pulling up over his blade to strike the far side of his head with the long edge, or lower the point and cut short-edge through his mouth. Beware his counters: he may drop his long point to your chest with a straight arm and step his left leg back, strike to your wrist, or bind and wind against you in turn, so keep your own point online and stay ready to change through.

records.briefDescription: The second of the six master strikes, the "Waker" is a rousing cross-cut driven with the long edge and an offline step that breaks the high guard Stier and wins the Eber and the strokes from below.
records.fullDescription: Begin with your Messer chambered on your right shoulder or set in the Schrankhut at your right leg, left foot forward, while your opponent waits in the Stier with his hilt before his head. As he threatens, leap with your right foot well out to your right side to carry yourself offline, and strike with the right (long) edge firmly onto his Messer to rouse and displace it. Indes, wind your point into his face so the cut flows straight into a thrust. Worked from the Schrankhut you can instead drop the hilt under your arm, bind his blade with the long edge, then turn the short edge onto his head. The stroke lives on its footwork — as the verse says, whoever wakes well with steps stretches many strokes — so the leap that clears his line matters as much as the cut. Keep the point busy throughout: after the bind you may hang it, wind into the hanging point with the long edge above, or strike short-edge to the head as the Messers spark together. It is roughly the Messer's answer to the Zwerchhau, a horizontal rousing displacement rather than a descending blow.
records.briefApplication: Reach for the Wecker to break an opponent waiting in the Stier or menacing from the Eber, stepping offline to rouse his blade and win the line above.
records.fullApplication: Reach for the Wecker to break an opponent waiting in the Stier or menacing from the Eber, stepping offline to rouse his blade and win the line above. It is your displacement of choice in the Zufechten when he holds a high threatening guard: the offline leap voids his point while your long edge wakes his Messer and your own point arrives at his face. Once you bind, work Indes rather than lingering — if he is weak in the bind, wind to his right side and take his neck; if he raises with the strong, strike again beneath his Messer to his head. You can also feint the Wecker to his left, then Durchwechseln and thrust to his right as he reaches for the parry, or wind into the hanging point and thrust with the long edge above. Expect a seasoned foe to break it: he may hang his point to your chest and push you off, Zucken his Messer free and cut over to your head, Durchgehen to your right to thrust, or answer with the Entrüsthau, winding high and striking your head. Guard against these by keeping your point online and your step complete, flowing straight from the rousing cut into your own winding or thrust before he can settle.

records.briefDescription: The third master strike, a high displacing cut that raises the hilt before your head into a hanging point and drops the short edge onto the head, breaking the Luginsland guard and every descending blow.
records.fullDescription: Begin with your left foot forward and the Messer held low, point toward the ground and the flat resting against your torso on the right side, much as in the Schrankhut. As he steps in and cuts down from the Luginsland, act in the Vor: leap well out to your right side and, as you leap, turn the Messer so the hilt rides high in front of your head with the thumb turned downward. This throws the point into a hanging line above you, the short (blunt) edge leading, while the raised hilt becomes a shield that covers your head. Drive the short edge down onto his upper opening, striking long from the arm and swinging the arm well around so the blow carries over his descending Messer. Deliver it with the strong of your Messer so you command the bind. If he comes sooner than you, displace with the same hanging turn out of his stroke, then strike long to his head. Should he prove too strong in the displacement, set the crosspiece or the guarding Nagel against his Messer, push it aside, and strike the Entrüsthau to another peak.
records.briefApplication: Choose the Entrüsthau to break the high Luginsland guard and any descending Oberhau, meeting the blow above with a hanging displacement that answers in the same tempo.
records.fullApplication: Choose the Entrüsthau to break the high Luginsland guard and any descending Oberhau, meeting the blow above with a hanging displacement that answers in the same tempo. Always aim for the four peaks: strike to the upper opening, and if he displaces, strike Indes to another peak, leaping far to the side with each cut so you stay covered behind your raised hilt. In the bind, feel his blade — if you catch his weak with your strong, mutate over his Messer to the neck; if you cannot, work Duplieren behind his blade with the short edge to the head, or twitch off and set the point on. It also breaks the Wecker: as he crosses in from his right, wind to your left, take the hanging point high, and strike the Entrüsthau to his head. The strike feeds naturally into overrunning, into winding the weak onto his Messer to strike long with the long edge, and into running in to take his Messer or wrestle. Feints serve well here, threatening one peak and striking another to dupe those who only displace and hew at the blade. Against it, beware the Sprechfenster and Langer Ort: a foe who holds a long point in your face breaks your feints, and a clean Schnitt over the arm punishes you if you strike carelessly around from the bind.

records.briefDescription: The fourth master strike, a crooked short-edge cut thrown from a low point-down guard up over a descending attack to strike the face, breaking the Eber and serving as the messer's rough analogue of the Krumphau.
records.fullDescription: As you close in the Zufechten, put your left foot forward and set your Messer with the point on the ground in front of you, your thumb turned underneath the grip. When he strikes an Oberhau down at your head, do not merely meet it: turn your Messer and drive the short (blunt) edge long from a fully stretched arm, up and over his descending Messer, so that it arrives against his face while your crossing blade constrains his stroke from above. The turn of the hand and the thumb beneath give the cut its crooked, over-binding character, which is why it works like the longsword's Krumphau — you catch his blade obliquely rather than trading force straight on. Keep the arm extended so the strike lands long and your point stays forward; the stretched arm and the forward point are what let this single short-edge action both foil his cut and threaten his head in one tempo. Delivered this way from the low point-down position, it breaks the Eber.
records.briefApplication: Choose the Zwinger to break the Eber and to answer a committed descending cut, meeting it over the top with a constraining short-edge strike to the face.
records.fullApplication: Choose the Zwinger to break the Eber and to answer a committed descending cut, meeting it over the top with a constraining short-edge strike to the face. Its verse warns of what a buffalo strikes or thrusts and of the one who trusts in changing — so it is your reply against a strong, brute-force fighter, the buffalo who overwhelms with power, whether he cuts from above or thrusts at you from the low Eber. Because you cross over his Messer rather than opposing it squarely, you both foil his stroke and land in a single tempo. The essential follow-up answers his most natural escape: if he defends cleverly and changes through below (Durchwechseln), do not chase his blade — remain with the Langer Ort thrust long into his face so he can do nothing and cannot come through underneath. The master notes that such breakings with the long point are better than the strokes themselves, since a committed cut cannot defend itself against a point already set in the face. From there work Indes: if he presses to clear the point, wind against his openings or fall into a Schnitt on his hands and arms. As a crooked over-binding action it shares the character of the Krumphau, and it is one of the four displacements — so heed the master's warning not to merely displace, but to threaten and work on from the bind.

records.briefDescription: The fifth master strike, a deceptive long-edge cut thrown from a high, stretched arm whose point sinks toward the opening, turning a threatened blow into a sudden thrust that waits for the face and chest.
records.fullDescription: Set yourself in the Luginsland: left foot forward, Messer held with a stretched arm high above your head, the long edge leading. As you close in the Zufechten, leap in with your right foot and strike from above with the long edge, but do not chop through. Keep your arm high and, as the blow travels, let your point sink downward so it hangs toward his face or chest, exactly as the verse says the Geférhau "with its point waits for the face and the chest." That high hand paired with a dropped, hanging point makes this a threatened cut that is really a thrust, which is what marks it as the Messer's rough analogue of the Schielhau. The deception lives in the changing-through: strike honestly and firmly against his Messer, and the instant he rises to set your stroke aside, let your point drop forward, change through beneath his blade (Durchwechseln), and shoot the point to his right side at the face with a fully stretched arm. The Nagel guards your hand as you extend that long point, so the stretched thrust rather than a committed chop carries the threat.
records.briefApplication: Choose the Geférhau when a foe waits in Luginsland or Bastei and you want a cut he must parry, so that his own defense opens the line for your changing-through thrust.
records.fullApplication: Choose the Geférhau when a foe waits in Luginsland or Bastei and you want a cut he must parry, so that his own defense opens the line for your changing-through thrust. Lecküchner lists it among the four displacements as the stroke that breaks the Bastei, and it works by baiting a reaction: you strike with real intent at his Messer, and because the threat is genuine he lifts to set it aside (Versetzen). That upward parry is the trap. Working Indes, the very moment he commits to rising you let the point fall forward, change through beneath his blade, and thrust to his right side at the face with a stretched arm, the "simultaneously" timing where Vor and Nach meet in a single tempo. Because the master then adds "do what you prefer," the thrust is only the first branch: if he finds your point and binds, you can wind against his blade or change through again to the other opening, or fall into the cuts and the close play. Its weakness is a foe who does not chase the feint; if he keeps his point online rather than reaching out to parry, there is nothing to change through, so make the opening cut convincing and read his hands before you let the point drop.

records.briefDescription: The sixth and newest master strike, a deceptive short-edge blow that begins as a long-edge cut, then winds high and beckons around to the head, undoing opponents who displace loosely and freely.
records.fullDescription: Stand with your left foot forward and chamber the Messer on your right shoulder (or set it in the Schranckhut with the right foot leading to work the mirror side). As your opponent waits in the Luginsland, drive a long stroke at him from the shoulder with a stretched arm, leading with the long edge. But do not let the blades meet: in the stroke, wind against his Messer, raise the hilt so your hand hangs high above, and turn the short edge over to strike his head. Indes, let the Messer sink down toward your body, go through to your left side with the point lowered, and beckon the short edge to the head on his other side. Because you switch edge and line before the blades ever spark together, the blow flicks around his cover like a beckoning wave of the hand. You can run it doubled to both sides, striking always with the short edge and going through underneath to cross over. If you choose not to go through, simply remain, wind to your left so the short edge sits below, and thrust to his face.
records.briefApplication: Choose the Wincker against a fighter who displaces freely and loosely, whose parry you can slip by turning to the short edge before the blades ever meet.
records.fullApplication: Choose the Wincker against a fighter who displaces freely and loosely, whose parry you can slip by turning to the short edge before the blades ever meet. Lecküchner calls it new, peculiar and good precisely because it punishes the free fighters who throw out displacements without working Indes, and it goes rightfully against anyone who parries in a crooked or wrong manner. It answers the high Luginsland especially well: your opening long-edge stroke draws his Versetzen, then you wind and flick the short edge high over his Messer to the head before he can settle any bind. Work everything Indes; the instant your point sinks, go through (Durchgehen) to the far side and beckon the short edge to his other opening, so the element threatens on both sides. If he covers the first head strike, do not chase it. Go high with the arm and thrust to his throat, chest, or face, winding again to renew the point should the first thrust fail, or fall to taking his weapon (Messer Nehmen) once you dominate his hands. Against a crooked displacer, turn your Messer before one sparks on the other and let the short edge arrive around his cover, so his parry closes on nothing.

records.briefDescription: The fundamental descending cut, struck straight down from above out of the right shoulder or the Luginsland — the plainest attack in the Messer, the one nearly every guard and master strike must answer.
records.fullDescription: Begin with your Messer chambered high, either resting on your right shoulder or held with a stretched arm high before your head in the Luginsland, the long (sharp) edge turned toward the man. Set your left foot forward. As you strike, leap in with your right foot and unwind the arm, driving the Messer down from above with the long edge leading and the arm stretched long, so the cut falls straight or diagonally onto the head, to his left or right side. Keep the point tracking your opponent throughout, so that where the edge does not land the point can follow: after the blow lands or is displaced, turn your Messer against his so the long edge stands above and the short edge below, and shoot the point long to his face or chest. This is the plainest stroke in the art, struck honestly and firmly, nothing else but a simple peasant stroke, yet its strength lies in reach and directness. Drive it long and committed in the Vor to force him to displace, then feel in the bind whether he is soft or hard before you continue your work.
records.briefApplication: Throw the Oberhau in the Zufechten to seize the Vor, forcing your opponent to answer from above and open himself to your follow-up work in the bind.
records.fullApplication: Throw the Oberhau in the Zufechten to seize the Vor, forcing your opponent to answer from above and open himself to your follow-up work in the bind. It is your default opening attack, the most direct way to menace the head and make him commit to a displacement. Because it is so plain, much of the art is organized to answer it: from the same high descent you can wrath it into the Zornhau and its Zornhau Ort, or sharpen it into one of the six master strikes, the hidden and refined strokes of the system. Expect it to be answered in kind. The Zornhau displaces it and shoots the point back; the Entrüsthau is made expressly to break the strokes struck from above downward; and the Zwinger turns the short edge long over your incoming cut to your face. Against a foe in the Luginsland or any raised guard, commit the cut long. Once the Messers spark together, do not merely stand parried but work Indes: feel soft or hard, then wind the point to his face, double behind his blade against the strong, or mutate to the lower opening against the weak. If he chases your Messer with his displacement, change through beneath and thrust to the far side; if he binds hard and strikes around, meet him with a cut from above into his arms. Never simply displace and wait, for whoever only displaces will be hurt by the whole art.

records.briefDescription: The Unterhau is the fundamental rising cut of the Messer, struck from below upward out of the low guards Eber and Bastei to displace an incoming blow and to threaten or slice the opponent's hands and arms.
records.fullDescription: Set yourself in a low guard such as the Eber, left foot forward and the hilt held low at your hip with the point angled up toward the opponent's face. Drive the cut from below upward along a straightened arm, letting the blade rise long into his hands, arm, or face while the point stays online the whole way. The long edge commonly leads the rising cut into the arm; striking from your left you can instead brace the thumb on the flat so the short edge goes forward, keeping the point driving true at the face. Cut with a gathering, twofold step — the lead foot steps in and the rear foot follows, the feet closing as you strike — so your weight climbs with the blade and the hilt reaches its highest just as the edge bites the arm. From that high hilt you can let the point fall into a thrust beneath his shoulder or chest, or, if the rising cut is displaced, remain on his Messer and wind to keep your point at his face. The stroke serves struck in full, as a half-stroke, or doubled from below.
records.briefApplication: Choose the Unterhau to answer or displace an attack from beneath and to menace the opponent's exposed hands and forearms, discouraging him from committing freely.
records.fullApplication: Choose the Unterhau to answer or displace an attack from beneath and to menace the opponent's exposed hands and forearms, discouraging him from committing freely. It rises naturally from the Eber and Bastei and is the reward of the Wecker, the displacement that obtains the Stier and the Eber and gains you the strokes from below. Use it in the Zufechten to threaten the hands as you close, or in the bind to slice upward into the arm: if he binds you from below, go Indes with the long edge onto his arm and press the cut downward or through his face. Should he displace the rising cut, do not linger — wind on his Messer to bring your point back to his face, Duplieren behind his blade to the far opening, or let the point sink into a thrust under his shoulder. Against a stubborn parry, Durchwechseln belongs especially to the strokes from below: feint the point to one side, drop it beneath his hilt, and thrust to the other. Beware that the low line invites the counter — an opponent who aims below can be overrun with Überlaufen, striking from above with a longer stroke and shooting the long point to your face so you cannot reach him from beneath, and the long point from the Luginsland or Bastei strips off strokes from below. Mask your intent and stay ready to change through the instant he sets his point against you.

records.briefDescription: The thrust with the point (Ort) — one of the three woundings with the cut and the slice — driving a leveled point into the face, throat, or chest out of winding, hanging, setting-off, and changing-through.
records.fullDescription: To thrust, extend the point straight at the man along a stretched arm, passing toward the opening so your body drives the Ort home. Most winding thrusts turn the thumb onto the flat of the Messer to steer and stiffen the point: as you go high with the hilt and wind against his blade, the short edge rides below and the long edge above, and the point stays leveled at his face. From the low guards you shoot the long point directly to the face, thumb above; from the bind you go high with the arm, wind against his Messer, and let the point fall to the nearest opening — the face, throat, chest, or stomach. The thrust seldom travels alone: it issues from the hanging point, from setting-off (Absetzen) as you catch his blade with the short edge so your own point stands ready against him, and from changing-through (Durchwechseln) as you drop the point beneath his weapon. Keep the arm long and the point online so that even a miss leaves you standing in the Langer Ort, threatening him and free to wind again.
records.briefApplication: Choose the thrust whenever his blade is occupied or offline — in the bind, or as he commits a cut — so your point reaches an opening before he can answer.
records.fullApplication: Choose the thrust whenever his blade is occupied or offline — in the bind, or as he commits a cut — so your point reaches an opening before he can answer. Against the Stier or Eber, go with the stretched long point Indes to his face, throat, or chest, falling with your rear foot well outside so he cannot thrust back. When he strikes at your Messer rather than your body, change through beneath his blade and thrust to the other peak; if he chases that with his displacement, change through again to the far side — thrust painfully from both sides. Against a committed cut from above, set off with the short edge or wind up to the Stier so the hilt shields your head, then step in and thrust to the face or chest. The thrust flows naturally out of winding and the hanging point, for whenever you go high with the arm in the bind, the Ort is already leveled at an opening. Do not merely parry a thrust, or the whole art will hurt you — set it aside on your own point kept online, or turn it away with the empty hand and seize his blade. His answers are also yours: he may change through under your point, set your thrust aside, or wind against it, so stay ready to double behind his blade, twitch to a new opening, or fall into a slice if he crowds your hilt.

records.briefDescription: The thrust that issues from the Zornhau: once your wrathful descending cut has displaced his stroke from above, you shoot the point forward into his face or chest with the long edge above.
records.fullDescription: When he strikes at your head from above on the right, answer with your own Zornhau from your right shoulder, cutting angrily downward so your blade meets his above and displaces it. Do not stop there: in that same instant, Indes, let your point shoot forward toward his face or chest and turn your Messer against his so the long edge stands above and the short edge below. This turn both threatens the thrust and keeps his blade off your line, your straight arm carrying the point long into the opening. If he becomes aware of the point and defends, wind it around to his left side toward the face, always keeping the long edge above; if he defends that too, pull the Messer up along the upper blade and strike to the other side of his head, taking away on the Messer. The action is plain enough that the master names it nothing but a simple peasant stroke, yet with it the Zornhau Ort breaks every stroke that comes from above.
records.briefApplication: Choose the Zornhau Ort to break any stroke that comes at you from above, meeting his cut with your own and instantly turning that displacement into a thrust.
records.fullApplication: Choose the Zornhau Ort to break any stroke that comes at you from above, meeting his cut with your own and instantly turning that displacement into a thrust. It answers an Oberhau in the Nach, yet the Indes shooting of the point seizes the Vor before he can recover, so you are never merely displacing, for the master warns that whoever only displaces is hurt by the whole art. If he feels the thrust and forces it aside, wind the point to his other side toward the face, keeping the long edge above; if he defends again, take away on the Messer and strike to the far side of his head, or lower the point between you and strike the cross stroke with the long edge to his right ear. You can also drop the point with the hilt held high and strike the short edge up into his face. Beware his counters: he may strike your hand at the wrist as the point comes in, or meet your thrust by lowering his own long point to your chest with a straight arm and a step back to push you off, and a Wecker struck against your Messer can likewise turn your point away and answer with his own thrust to your face.

records.briefDescription: The Vor, or "Before," is the initiative: you come with your stroke sooner than your opponent so that he must displace, one of the three timing words the master calls the keep of the entire art.
records.fullDescription: The Vor is not a single cut but the act of seizing the tempo, so you take it the moment you enter the Zufechten: rather than standing still and waiting for his strokes, you drive a committed stroke into the nearest opening before your opponent can move. Set out from a forward guard — the left foot leading as in the Luginsland, or the point dropped to the ground in the Schranckhut — and as you go before, leap in with the foot toward the side you strike so your whole body drives the blow. Let the long edge lead and the point run forward, aimed at a definite peak, so that he has no choice but to displace your Messer rather than answer with a stroke of his own. The instant your blow lands or is met, you do not pause: you keep working Indes with the Messer in front of you, flowing straight into further strokes, thrusts, winding, or cuts so he can never come to any work of his own. This unbroken pressure, taken sooner than he and never surrendered, is what the master means when he says you have acquired the Vor.
records.briefApplication: Take the Vor whenever you close in the Zufechten and want to dictate the fight, striking first so your opponent is put on the defensive and forced to react to you.
records.fullApplication: Take the Vor whenever you close in the Zufechten and want to dictate the fight, striking first so your opponent is put on the defensive and forced to react to you. It answers a hesitant or waiting foe: attack a tempo before he settles, force his displacement, then stay in the war (Krieg), feeling in the bind whether he is soft or hard and working Indes to the next opening with winding, Duplieren, or a cut so he never recovers. The Vor is countered by his Nach: if he comes sooner than you, or if you merely displace and stand there, the initiative passes to him, and the master warns that whoever only displaces will be beaten by the whole art. But losing it is not the end, because you can take the Vor back from him with your Nach: displace his blow and, in the very same instant, work Indes so skillfully that you seize the tempo again and do not let him come to any work. This is why Indes binds the two together, living inside both Vor and Nach, and why Nachreisen, Absetzen, and shooting the long point are all ways to steal the initiative back the moment he over-commits or leaves a tempo open.

records.briefDescription: The counter-time in Lecküchner's timing: the responding tempo you work in when the opponent comes sooner and forces you to displace, whereupon you reply instantly and take the Vor back from him.
records.fullDescription: Nach is a state of timing rather than a single cut, so you hold it in readiness: stand in a forward guard such as the Luginsland, left foot leading, your shield — that is, the displacement — held before your head, and never stand still merely watching his blade. When he comes sooner than you with a stroke and you must displace it, meet his Messer with the long edge, the point kept online and the Nagel guarding your hand. The instant the two blades meet, feel through the bind whether he is soft or hard, and without pause drive your own work Indes: shoot the point long to his face or chest, wind over his blade, slice the long edge down into his arm, or hang the point over his Messer and thrust to the far opening. The whole art of the Nach lies in that immediate reply, for as the master warns, who displaces only will be hurt by the entire art.
records.briefApplication: Work in the Nach whenever the opponent has seized the Vor and strikes first: displace his attack and answer Indes so the initiative flows straight back to you.
records.fullApplication: Work in the Nach whenever the opponent has seized the Vor and strikes first: displace his attack and answer Indes so the initiative flows straight back to you. It is your reply to anyone who commits — above all the fencer who throws a long stroke and then recovers. If his cut falls short or misses, do not wait; strike to him after into the nearest opening before he can raise his Messer again, which is the heart of Nachreisen. If instead you catch him in the bind, read soft or hard through the feeling of the Messer: when he is soft, shoot the point to his face, wind over to the opening, or use Mutieren to hang the point over his blade and thrust to the lower opening; when he is hard, use Duplieren to go high with the arm and strike behind his blade to the head. Should he change through beneath your displacement, follow with the Langer Ort so he can do nothing. Beware that the Nach can be turned against you: a fencer who only reaches to displace is easily drawn by a feint, so keep your shield, the displacement, before your head, never chase his blade blindly, and let every parry carry its reply, or he will take the Vor back from you in the very same moment.

records.briefDescription: Indes is the decisive instant in the bind — the moment your Messer touches his, when you feel whether he is soft or hard and wind, strike, thrust, or slice to the next opening before he can act.
records.fullDescription: Indes is not a stroke but a faculty of timing you exercise the instant your blade meets his in the bind. As the two Messers spark together, keep your point online toward his face and read the pressure running down the blade through your strong against his weak — this is the feeling of the Messer (Empfindung). If he is soft in the bind, drive Indes forward into the nearest opening: shoot the point, wind so the long edge stands above, or press a slice into his arm before he recovers. If he is hard and shoving against you, do not fight the pressure but yield Indes, winding to a new angle, changing through beneath his blade, or twitching off to another peak. The whole action is a single tempo — you feel and answer in the same moment his weapon commits, your feet leaping offline as your hand turns the Messer, point, long edge, or short edge working while the Nagel guards your hand. Never pause to look at his weapon and displace only; that hesitation is exactly the tempo Indes is made to steal.
records.briefApplication: Work Indes the instant you feel the bind — it turns a mere displacement into an attack, letting you beat him to the next opening instead of standing still to parry.
records.fullApplication: Work Indes the instant you feel the bind — it turns a mere displacement into an attack, letting you beat him to the next opening instead of standing still to parry. It is the master key to the whole system: whether you hold the Vor, coming with a stroke sooner so he must displace, or the Nach, forced to displace his committed blow, Indes is how you keep working, and with it your Nach steals the Vor back from him. The moment counts most in the war, the close exchange after a Zornhau or Wecker: feel whether he is soft or hard, then wind the point to his face, double behind his blade, mutate the upper bind into a thrust below, or twitch off and change through to the other peak. Against a fencer who only wants to displace and watch your Messer, Indes is his undoing, for his hesitation is the very tempo you take — this is also why the feints and the settings on succeed, since the blades spark and you commit before he can recover his guard. Its only real counter is better Indes: if he winds or slices in the same instant, you must feel it and act first again, because whoever owns the tempo owns the bind. Never let the bind go static — the fencer who pauses to look loses the entire art.

records.briefDescription: Displacing is the parry of Lecküchner's Messer system, meeting an incoming cut or thrust so that the very act of defending turns your point online and threatens the opponent rather than merely blocking.
records.fullDescription: There is no single fixed posture for Versetzen; you displace from whatever guard you stand in, but the master's model is a displacement that strikes rather than waits. Against a cut coming from above from his right shoulder, strike from your own right side, also from above, angrily meeting his blade to turn it aside, and in the same tempo let your point shoot forward to his face or chest, rolling the Messer so the long edge stands above and the short edge below. Carry the hilt raised and well in front of your head — the master calls the displacement your shield, so it must cover the line it defends. Step or leap offline as you catch the blow, moving out of the stroke to your right so his force passes you while your point stays aimed at an opening. The strongest form is simply to set the Langer Ort in his way: extend the point long against the man so his cut or thrust runs onto it and cannot land, defending and threatening in one stretched motion.
records.briefApplication: Use Versetzen whenever you must answer an attack you did not lead, but never as a bare block: displace so that you seize the Vor back with your Nach in the same instant.
records.fullApplication: Use Versetzen whenever you must answer an attack you did not lead, but never as a bare block: displace so that you seize the Vor back with your Nach in the same instant. The Recital warns that whoever only displaces will be hurt by the entire art — a fencer who stands and waits, watching another man's strokes, is beaten in spite of his skill. So the moment your Messer meets his, work Indes and feel whether he is soft or hard in the bind. If he is hard and strong in the displacement, wind your point high to his face, or double behind his blade to the head; if he is soft or weak, mutate over his Messer to the lower opening. If he chases your blade with his own displacement, change through beneath it to the far opening, or twitch your point off and thrust to the other peak. When he strikes around from the displacement, fall with the long edge over his arm and cut. Displacing also names the four displacements — the Wecker, Entrüsthau, Zwinger and Geferhau — the master strokes that break the four guards, so that you unseat a stance with a threatening cut rather than a passive parry. Beware the same fault in yourself: an opponent who displaces freely, or in a crooked and wrong manner, invites the Wincker and the feint, and the long point breaks any defense that leaves its own point idle.

records.briefDescription: A technique of the Nach in which you follow, or chase, the opponent's committed or withdrawing stroke, striking into the opening he leaves before he can bring his Messer back into guard.
records.fullDescription: Stand in the guard of Luginsland with your left foot forward, arm stretched high before your head and the long edge toward the man, watching him closely rather than committing first. When he throws a long stroke from his right shoulder that falls short, wait for the instant his Messer sinks toward the ground and can no longer reach you; then leap in with your right foot and cut from above with the long edge into the opening on his right side, arriving sooner than he can raise his Messer to guard again. Should he recover and bind, stay firm with the long edge pressed on his Messer and feel at once whether he is soft or hard; the moment one blade sparks on the other, step your left foot well behind his right and strike to his head, or lay the long edge on his arm and press the cut downward, or slice through his face. You can also chase from the Bastei, avoiding his stroke to the side and thrusting with a stretched arm over his Messer, winding the point firmly to his face if he displaces. Chase on either side, bringing cuts, windings, or thrusts out of the same motion.
records.briefApplication: Use Nachreisen against a foe who fights with long, free strokes that overcommit or miss, striking the recovery gap before he can bring his Messer back to guard.
records.fullApplication: Use Nachreisen against a foe who fights with long, free strokes that overcommit or miss, striking the recovery gap before he can bring his Messer back to guard. It is the art of the Nach: rather than displacing, you stand patient in Luginsland or Bastei, let his stroke spend itself, and answer in the empty tempo as his weapon falls away. It punishes the free fighters who swing wide and withdraw from the man, and it serves equally when your own chasing stroke has been displaced, so long as you remain on his blade, feel for soft or hard, and let your work follow Indes. If he goes high and binds you from below, go simultaneously with the long edge onto his arm and press the cut down, or cut through his face. If he strikes an Entrüsthau around your head from the bind, meet it Indes with your own Entrüsthau forward under his Messer to his neck, or raise the hilt and drop the point to his chest to push him back. From the same chase you can wind the point firmly to his face or shoot a stretched-arm thrust. The chase is itself broken by the Bogen: the man you are chasing can bow under your Messer, catch your stroke on the flat with the short edge against you, then overwind and thrust to your cheek in return.

records.briefDescription: Overrunning answers a low attack with a longer, higher one: you meet a blow from below not by parrying but by striking over it from above, so your reach lands your point while his low blow falls short.
records.fullDescription: As you close in the Zufechten and your opponent strikes at you from below with a low cut or half-stroke, do not displace it. Mark the instant his blow rises toward you and answer it by striking from your right shoulder from above, driving the cut out long with the long edge leading and shooting the point straight to his face. Keep the arm stretched so the Messer travels over the top of his attack; because your line runs higher and longer, you set on to his face while his low blow falls short and cannot reach you from below. Should he lift from below and displace your descending point, do not pull back: remain with the long edge lying firmly on his Messer and, in that same instant, go high with the arm, wind, and let the point hang down into his face over his defense. Throughout, the higher hand and the longer arm dominate the low line, so it is reach and the commanding upper line, not a parry that meets his blow, that decide the exchange.
records.briefApplication: Choose Überlaufen whenever an opponent commits to a low cut or thrust from beneath: rather than parry, out-reach him from above so your point lands first.
records.fullApplication: Choose Überlaufen whenever an opponent commits to a low cut or thrust from beneath: rather than parry, out-reach him from above so your point lands first. The principle is "who aims below, overrun him" — a high, extended line covers more ground than a rising one, so a strong strike from above wins the line by superior reach rather than by trading a parry. Do not fall into displacing; the master warns that merely parrying leaves you hurt, so treat the overrun as a counter in the Nach, striking as his low blow travels. Your safeguard against his answer is built in: if he rises to displace your descending point, keep the long edge firm on his Messer and work Indes — go high with the arm, wind, and hang the point into his face, flowing straight into the Winden and the hangings (Hängen). In the same chapter the master also overruns with the Entrüsthau against a foe in the Luginsland, going over his Messer with the hilt, winding and raising the pommel to strike with the hilt or thrust with the armed hand, then seizing the neck to throw him over your leg. Guard against the master's own breaking against these overrunning plays: he turns his edge to cut and works the point, and if you crowd in to grapple he pushes you off and twitches (Zucken) his Messer free.

records.briefDescription: Setting off is a single-time displacing counter in which you wind the opponent's cut or thrust aside with your short edge while your point stays online, so one action both deflects him and threatens his face.
records.fullDescription: Absetzen is the fifth of the further elements, worked from the four guards but taught most clearly from the Eber. Come out of the Zufechten and set your left foot forward, holding the Messer low on your right side in the Eber with the point angled up toward the man, and deliberately expose your left opening as bait. When he thrusts at that opening, wind your Messer over to your left side against his thrust so that the short edge comes onto his blade, and set his point aside — but do not chase it away. The same wind that turns him must leave your own point standing against his face or body, so a single motion defends and threatens at once; then drive your thrust home to his face or chest. Against a descending stroke from the same Eber, instead go high and wind to your left so the hilt rises before your head into the Stier, catching his cut above, then step in with the forward foot and thrust. Keep the arm firm and the point true throughout: the deflection and the threat are one tempo, not two.
