You can perform it on both sides, from any of the four guards, against strokes and thrusts alike.
records.briefApplication: Choose Absetzen when an opponent commits to a cut or thrust and you want to defend and counter in a single tempo rather than merely parrying.
records.fullApplication: Choose Absetzen when an opponent commits to a cut or thrust and you want to defend and counter in a single tempo rather than merely parrying. It embodies the master's warning that whoever only displaces will be hurt by the whole art: rather than knocking the blade away and then attacking, you turn his line aside while your point never leaves his face, so the Nach becomes the Vor in one motion. Bait him from a guard such as the Eber, exposing an opening; the instant he fills it, wind and set off, working Indes so his own committed weapon carries him onto your waiting point. Because that point stays online, he cannot safely Durchwechseln beneath your blade — the very error that punishes a loose set-off whose point drifts wide. Its chief danger is the deceptive stroke: a Geférhau feints at your Messer, and as you rise to set aside he lets his point drop, changes through, and thrusts to your other opening. Guard against this by keeping the displacement small and the point honest rather than over-committing to the parry. If your setting-off thrust is itself displaced, flow on into the hangings and winding against the openings, or double behind his blade to the nearest opening.

records.briefDescription: A deceptive point action in which you drop your Messer's point beneath the opponent's blade the moment he reaches for your steel to bind or parry, then thrust through to the far opening before he finds steel.
records.fullDescription: Durchwechseln lives on the point rather than the edge, so keep your arm long and your Messer's tip alive. A clear form: come in the Zufechten and strike a long stroke from above to his head, or set your left foot forward and hold the Langer Ort against his face. Then watch where his blade travels. If he strikes at your Messer to bind or beat it aside, and not at your body, Indes let your point sink down and through beneath his blade before the steel meets, then drive it up to the opposite opening, his face or chest on the far side, with a stretched arm. Should he chase your point with his displacement, simply change through again to the other side; work it on both sides. From long rising strokes the same holds: with your feet drawing together and a straight arm, feint as if to shoot the point at his right side, then Indes let the tip sway through low at his hilt and thrust to his left. As you change you may also strike the short edge over his Messer, let the point fall, and cut through his head with the long edge. Move with care throughout, so he cannot set on or draw after while your point passes under.
records.briefApplication: Choose Durchwechseln against opponents who chase your steel, striking to your Messer to bind or parry rather than to your body, and punish the opening they abandon.
records.fullApplication: Choose Durchwechseln against opponents who chase your steel, striking to your Messer to bind or parry rather than to your body, and punish the opening they abandon. It is the natural partner of the Geferhau: as you strike that perilous cut and he goes high to set it aside, let the point fall forward, change through, and thrust to his face with a stretched arm. But read the bind first, because Lecküchner's decision rule governs everything. If he binds or displaces yet lets his point drift out to the side, off your face and your openings, change through merrily; if instead he keeps his point online and threatening your face, do not change through. Remain on the Messer and wind or work to the nearest opening, lest he set on or draw after you as your point crosses. That same principle names the counter to Durchwechseln itself: an opponent who holds the Langer Ort straight at your face breaks the change-through, for he simply stays with the long point and thrusts as you pass beneath, stepping his rear foot wide to reach further. Where your change lands and he is soft, flow onward, doubling behind his blade with Duplieren, winding for a cleaner line, or twitching off with Zucken should he bind hard again. Perform it on both sides, always with great care so no one sets on against you mid-change.

records.briefDescription: A deceptive bind element in which you let your Messer weave and run off out of the bind from both sides, drawing the opponent to chase your blade so you can strike Indes into the opening he uncovers.
records.fullDescription: Begin from the bind, having closed in the Zufechten and bound close on his Messer. Rather than press, let the blade flow: weave it from side to side out of the bind, exactly as a woman unspools yarn from both sides, keeping your thumb pressed down on the flat of the Messer throughout so it turns freely. As you weave, sink your weight as if you meant to sit down, letting the Messer run off and down from both sides so the bind's pressure spills away and your point rides loose and free. Keep the motion continuous while you feel for the instant he commits. The moment you see him follow your weaving Messer with his displacement, act Indes and throw a Feler: show to one side and land on whichever side you can surest reach him. Or, as the Messer runs off, strike quickly to the lower opening and instantly again to the upper; or drive the point to his chest, then strike skillfully back to the first opening.
records.briefApplication: Use Ablaufen from the bind to bait a defensive opponent into chasing your blade, then strike Indes into the opening his displacement uncovers.
records.fullApplication: Use Ablaufen from the bind to bait a defensive opponent into chasing your blade, then strike Indes into the opening his displacement uncovers. It answers the man who only displaces — the master warns that whoever relies on parrying alone will be hurt by the whole art — because your weaving, sinking Messer invites him to follow, and the instant he commits to chasing it he stands out of position. Choose it when the bind is even and you would rather draw a mistake than force one. As his displacement follows your blade, work Indes: throw a Feler and land on whichever side you can surest reach him, or run the point off and strike the lower opening then the upper, or thrust to the chest and return to the first opening. From here you flow into Winden against the openings, into Durchwechseln if he over-covers one line, or into Duplieren should he catch your strike hard. In the armed manner, the free hand laid on the blade, the same running off on both sides sets up thrusts, cuts and strokes: overrun his Messer, seize him by the neck, and finish with the armed hand. The bait only works if he takes it — against a patient man who keeps his point online in your face and refuses to chase, you draw out no opening, so break off and bind anew rather than weave onto a waiting point.

records.briefDescription: Übernehmen is a bind-dominating action from the hanging point: you drive your crosspiece over the opponent's Messer, press it aside, go high with your arm, and strike behind his blade to his head.
records.fullDescription: Übernehmen begins in the Zufechten, when you and your opponent close and both settle into the hanging point, Messers crossed and bound with the points hanging toward one another. From here you take his blade over from above. Standing on his right in the bind, lay your crosspiece over onto his Messer toward his left and push his blade across to his right with your own; as you do, step well around to his left with your right foot and, driving your arm high, strike behind his blade to his head with the blunt short edge. On the other side, when you stand on his left, bring the crosspiece or hilt onto his blade toward his right, push his Messer to his left, step your left foot forward to his right side, and strike his head with the long edge. Throughout, keep your hand covered behind the Nagel, move with the cross to master his weapon, and use whichever edge the side demands. The high arm and the crosspiece are what let you dominate above and clear the path for the strike behind his Messer.
records.briefApplication: Choose Übernehmen when both of you have settled into the hanging point in the bind and you want to take control of his Messer from above and strike behind it.
records.fullApplication: Choose Übernehmen when both of you have settled into the hanging point in the bind and you want to take control of his Messer from above and strike behind it. It thrives in that mutual hanging bind where neither point yet threatens cleanly: rather than wrestle for the center, you overpower his blade with your crosspiece, push it offline, and step around to strike the head he leaves uncovered. The action feeds naturally into taking his weapon — as you take over, drop your empty left hand onto his hilt and pull downward to wrench the Messer from him, or reach through his Messer to trap it with the empty hand — so Übernehmen doubles as an entry to Messer Nehmen, and it can flow onward into winding and a thrust to the face if he stiffens. Work it Indes, feeling whether he is soft or hard as you push. Respect its breaks: the master's own remedy is Durchgehen, going through — as you push and wind up your strike he twitches his Messer close to his body with a lowered point (Zucken) and beats you to the ear, or, the surer break, he goes high under your Messer and sets his point on your neck. Because twitching and going through undo it, commit only once you feel his Messer yield to your cross, and keep your point ready to wind should he slip free.

records.briefDescription: The Bow is a bow-shaped hanging displacement — hilt raised, point lowered, arm and Messer curved into a shield before your head — used to catch a stroke swung around at your head, worked twofold from both sides.
records.fullDescription: To form the Bow, hold your Messer low on your left side, above the knee, with the point toward the man. When he strikes or binds around from his right to your left, bow the Messer in toward your body: raise the hilt, let the point sink a little, turn the thumb underneath the grip, and set the blunt short edge toward yourself, so that your arm and blade curve into a rounded shield — your displacement — carried well before your head. As the two Messers spark together, catch his stroke on the flat of your hanging blade. Then work Indes: step clear of the line with a twofold step, carrying both feet around toward his open side, and strike through his head. The Bow is worked twofold from both sides — mirror it on the right, thumb above and point toward the ground with the blunt short edge to him, bowing up under his Messer, then stepping around to strike the far side of his head. Because you hang rather than meet force squarely, the shield lets his stroke slide off while your point and hilt stay poised to wind.
records.briefApplication: Choose the Bow against a rough stroke that comes around at your head or neck: bend under his Messer, catch it on the shield, and step around behind him to strike.
records.fullApplication: Choose the Bow against a rough stroke that comes around at your head or neck: bend under his Messer, catch it on the shield, and step around behind him to strike. It answers wide peasant blows and the Wecker that swing around the head, where meeting edge-to-edge would lose the exchange — instead you hang, let the force spend itself on the flat, and use the twofold step to leave the line entirely. Once you have displaced, work Indes: wind over his Messer to his right side and step behind him to strike his head, or thrust to his cheek or throat as the winding opens. The Bow is also a doorway to the close game, for many Messer-takings flow from it — leap under his blade with the bow, seize over his Messer with your free hand, and press into his wrist so he must drop the weapon. You may likewise use it to catch a Nachreisen when your own stroke has missed, hanging under his blade with the shield before your head. Beware the counters: an alert opponent steps offline and strikes your head as your direct stroke comes out of the bow, or winds and thrusts to your face; he may even turn his short edge onto your Messer, then roll to the long edge and cut through your head. Guard the wind by going over his weak with the hilt and striking or thrusting first.

records.briefDescription: The Messer's dominant point-forward position: your arm stretched full and the point driven long into the opponent's face or chest so he can do nothing but react — the best defense in the whole art and your surest close.
records.fullDescription: Extend the point long by stretching your arm fully so the Messer reaches out toward the opponent's face or chest, keeping your body behind the steel. Commonly you stand with the left foot forward and the thumb lying above on the flat of the Messer, the point held online and threatening; either edge may lead depending on how you arrived — the long edge above when you wind up from below, the short (blunt) edge above when you set on out of the Zwinger. You reach the Langer Ort from the guards, shooting it long from the Bastei or down from the Luginsland, out of the Zwinger, and out of every winding and hanging point, finishing with the arm long rather than short. Because the stretched point outreaches his stroke, he cannot come in without first dealing with the steel already in his face, and your reach lets you thrust, strike, or cut from it the instant he commits. Stay balanced and light in the legs, stepping to keep the point on his centre, so that whatever he attempts you meet it Indes with the point.
records.briefApplication: Use the Langer Ort to seize and hold the initiative, forcing the opponent to react to your extended point while you stay safely covered behind it.
records.fullApplication: Use the Langer Ort to seize and hold the initiative, forcing the opponent to react to your extended point while you stay safely covered behind it. The master names it the best defense in the Messer: it breaks strike and thrust alike, for a bare stroke cannot protect itself once your point already fills his face, and if he tries to win the Vor you take it from him and work Indes according to the Nach. Choose it whenever you want the surest close, and above all against a waiting guard — go with the long stretched point to the face of a man in the Eber or Stier, or shoot it as a setting-off (Absetzen) to his nearest opening when he strikes from above. If he answers by binding, striking your Messer aside, or changing through below, let the point drop and change through (Durchwechseln) to thrust the other side, or wind into the hanging point and thrust from there; if he stays high and hard in the bind, follow with Duplieren or go through. Against his feints and the Entrüsthau, break them with the long point held as a Sprechfenster and seek the openings in a masterly way. Its chief risk is over-committing on the single forward line, so cover his change-through and winding, keep stepping offline, and if you fail with the point wind into the Stier and be first again to his face.

records.briefDescription: The seventh element: in a firm bind, sharply twitch (jerk) your Messer back off his blade and immediately strike or thrust to a different opening, deceiving an opponent who binds hard and displaces strongly.
records.fullDescription: Twitching lives in the bind. Come into the Zufechten and strike firmly — for instance bind with the Entrüsthau onto his Messer at his left side — then, as the blades spark together, twitch a little back with your arm, jerking your Messer sharply off his to break the pressure. Keep the movement small and quick, sometimes drawing the weapon toward you only to the middle of the blade rather than fully away. As you twitch you must wind your Messer against his so the long edge rides above, keeping your point online; then thrust out of that same motion to another opening — his face, throat, or chest. Set your feet with a twofold step offline, often to his right, so your body clears his blade even as your point returns. From the Bastei you may twitch your whole body out of an incoming stroke; from the Luginsland, twitch the Messer toward you, raise the hilt to your head with the short edge turned inward and the point sinking to your left, then set the point into his throat and push him back.
records.briefApplication: Choose Zucken against a master who binds hard and displaces strongly, using the jerk off his blade to dupe his pressure and hit an opening he has left.
records.fullApplication: Choose Zucken against a master who binds hard and displaces strongly, using the jerk off his blade to dupe his pressure and hit an opening he has left. The element is numerous and various, but its logic is constant: when he commits his strength to the bind or reaches to seize your blade, deny him the contact he wants. If you strike from above to his head and he moves to displace, twitch your Messer to yourself before he binds and thrust to the far peak; if he has already bound and waits to see whether you will pull back, remain on the blade, twitch only to the middle, then thrust again quickly to his face or chest. Work Indes throughout — the twitch and the thrust are one tempo. If the thrust does not land cleanly, flow on with Duplieren or let the Messer run through and strike the far opening with the long or short edge, and you may also twitch through to change through or cut. It pairs naturally with Durchwechseln, since both feed on a man who over-commits to the bind. Its counter is to refuse the disengage: as he goes high with the hilt to twitch, drive your point firmly into his face and raise your arm, following his Messer with the hanging point so he can neither come off your blade nor twitch through.

records.briefDescription: Abschneiden, the ninth main element, is a family of four slicing cuts - two from above and two from below - pressed edge-first into the opponent's arms and wrists in the bind to wound him and drive him off.
records.fullDescription: There are four cuts, two from above and two from below, and each is a shearing press of the edge onto the arm rather than a struck hew. For the upper cuts against a foe who whips around out of the bind - say with the Entrüsthau to your other side - leap out of his stroke with your left foot to his right side and fall with the long (sharp) edge over his arm, pressing the slice away from you; when instead you both lie at the ear and he strikes toward your other ear, cut with the short edge into the inside of his arm. For the two lower cuts against a foe who runs in with a high, stretched arm, turn your Messer so the thumb is below and drive the edge under his hilt onto his arm, pressing firmly upward as you slice - the long edge when he comes in on your left, the short edge when he comes in on your right. Keep your hand and point controlling his weapon throughout, so the slice both bites and shoves; performed well, you can bring these cuts into every bind.
records.briefApplication: Choose Abschneiden when the opponent strikes around out of the bind or runs in with a stretched arm - lay your edge on his arm and slice to wound him and drive him off.
records.fullApplication: Choose Abschneiden when the opponent strikes around out of the bind or runs in with a stretched arm - lay your edge on his arm and slice to wound him and drive him off. The upper cuts answer fighters who leave the bind and swing to your other opening, as with the Entrüsthau, while the lower cuts answer those who run in high to grapple or close; because the slice both wounds and displaces, it punishes these committed actions safely. Work Indes: feel the instant he strikes around or runs in and fall on the arm before his blow lands. The cuts flow into one another - having sliced upward from below with the short edge, turn the Messer around on his arm and drop the upper cut over the same arm, changing low to high. From a lower cut you can step to his left side, let the hilt pass through below, and roll the long edge over into a cut from above, or carry the slice on into his neck or chest; it sits close to Hände Drücken and the Winden and can be reached out of any bind. Its own answer is Messer nehmen: cut into his outstretched right arm and he may pin your blade with his hilt, reach his free hand over behind your hilt, and pull to strip your Messer - so drive the slice home and keep your hilt strong rather than leaving the cutting arm hanging for him to seize.

records.briefDescription: The hangings: from the bind you let your point hang over the opponent's blade from above (out of the Stier) or under it from below (out of the Eber) so it still threatens his face while the strong shelters your hand.
records.fullDescription: Work the hangings from the bind. For the upper hanging, stand in the Stier: raise your hilt high beside your head with the arm lifted, so the point hangs downward over the opponent's blade and stays aimed at his face or chest. The strong of the Messer, guarded by the Nagel, rests on his blade and shelters your hand while the weak keeps the threat. Standing on your right side, if he strikes from above at your left, wind against his stroke with the short edge on his Messer, staying in the Stier; should he set the thrust aside, remain on the blade, wind back to your right with the flat on his Messer, and thrust from above at his face. Working from your left side, lead instead with the long edge. For the lower hanging, take the Eber on either side: hold the hilt low and let the point hang up from beneath his Messer, still menacing his face. There are four hangings in all, the two upper from the Stier and the two lower from the Eber, the two from above and the two from below, and from these four you bring eight windings, delivering a stroke, a thrust, or a cut from each.
records.briefApplication: Reach for the hangings in the bind when you want to stay sheltered yet keep your point online: the strong guards your hand while the hanging point threatens his face.
records.fullApplication: Reach for the hangings in the bind when you want to stay sheltered yet keep your point online: the strong guards your hand while the hanging point threatens his face. Use the upper hanging to catch a stroke from above; as his cut lands, go high with the arm and hang the point over his Messer to his face or chest, even hanging it into his chest to push him from you, or driving on with the Entrüsthau to his head. Feel whether he is soft or hard, for the master binds the hangings to the openings and to the play of soft and hard: if he is soft, thrust in with the hanging point; if he resists, wind. From the four hangings flow the eight windings, each yielding a stroke, a thrust, or a cut, and the hangings feed the Mutieren, where you hang your point over his Messer, take the arm high, and thrust to the other opening, as well as the Übernehmen and Messer nehmen worked from the hanging point. Watch the counters: if he twitches out of the hanging point with Zucken to strike your ear, go with your point firmly to his face and do not let him leave the Messer; if he hangs his point at your face, let your Messer drop below his arm and rise with the Langer Ort, or wind against him in the hanging point and thrust.

records.briefDescription: Winden is the seventeenth main element: in the bind you turn your Messer around the opponent's blade to bring your point and either edge online against his four openings, the heart of the close play.
records.fullDescription: Winden begins the instant your blade meets his in the bind, usually after a displacing cut such as the Zornhau or Wecker. Rather than pull back, stay firmly on his Messer and rotate around his blade: go high with the arm and raise the hilt, turning the Messer so the long edge stands above and the short edge below, with your thumb pressed on the flat for leverage. This carries your point online to his face or chest along his blade. If he becomes aware of the point and defends, wind again to the other side, so the long edge is now below and the short edge above, and thrust or strike from there. Each turn keeps your point threatening while changing which edge and what leverage you bring to bear. Through the contact you feel Indes whether he is soft or hard on the Messer, and you wind on both sides, working the point around against his four openings. This working of the point in the bind is what the master calls the Krieg, the war.
records.briefApplication: Wind whenever your cut is caught in the bind, using contact and Indes to turn your point against his openings rather than merely displacing.
records.fullApplication: Wind whenever your cut is caught in the bind, using contact and Indes to turn your point against his openings rather than merely displacing. The master warns that whoever only displaces will be hurt by the whole art, so treat every bind as the doorway to the Krieg and feel through the blades whether he is soft or hard. If he is soft, wind high and shoot the point to his face; if he presses hard and displaces that thrust, go high to the other side and thrust under his arm to the chest, then follow to the next opening he leaves. This same feeling of soft and hard chooses between Duplieren, doubling behind his blade against the strong, and Mutieren, sinking the point over his blade to the lower opening against the weak; the Hängen and the Langer Ort flow out of the same winding. Winding answers a stubborn, strong bind and any free or crooked displacement, since from the contact you can always send the point above or below. It is countered in turn by winding against your winding, by changing through (Durchwechseln) beneath your point, or by twitching (Zucken) off the blade to strike a fresh opening before your turn completes.

records.briefDescription: Duplieren is an Indes counter worked against the strong of the opponent's Messer: right after the bind you go high with the arm, stay on his blade, and immediately strike again behind it with the short edge.
records.fullDescription: You reach Duplieren straight out of a strong bind, not as a fresh strike. Come in with a forceful cut and feel him displace hard, strong against strong. In the plainest form you have struck from your left and bound on his Messer with the long edge; now, without leaving the blade, shoot your arm quickly high, keep your Messer lying on his so the bind is never broken, and snap the short (blunt) edge behind his blade to strike his head, doubling the very stroke he thought he had parried. If instead you both came down from the right shoulder and he meets your strong, wind the hilt in under your right arm, go high with the arm the same way, and strike with the long edge behind his blade to the head. Either way the defining action is the same: stay glued to his strong, ride the arm high above him, and deliver the second cut behind his blade before he can free it. Drive it from wrist and arm rather than winding away, and let his own hard parry give you the frame you strike around.
records.briefApplication: Choose Duplieren the instant you feel the opponent parry your strong strike hard and strong, striking again behind his blade before he can recover or riposte.
records.fullApplication: Choose Duplieren the instant you feel the opponent parry your strong strike hard and strong, striking again behind his blade before he can recover or riposte. It is the answer to the strong of his Messer, and it pairs with Mutieren as a matched set the master frames as "double from above and mutate from below": in the bind you feel Indes whether he is soft or hard, and against a hard, strong displacement you double, while against a weak, yielding one you mutate down to the lower opening instead. Because you never leave his blade, doubling defeats the fencer who trusts a firm parry — the harder he presses, the more surely his strong holds nothing behind it. It flows naturally out of strong descending strokes like the Zornhau, and it also lives among the Entrüsthau plays: when your Entrüsthau's strong catches the weak of his Messer and you cannot mutate, work the doubling behind his blade to his head. If your doubled cut does not land, cut through his face, chase firmly to the next opening, or fall back to going-through or changing-through. It fails against an opponent who is soft in the bind or who slips the bind entirely, since then the strong is not there to strike around, and Mutieren or a changing-through serves better.

records.briefDescription: Mutieren transforms an upper bind into a thrust to the opponent's lower opening by winding over his blade and sinking the point in, worked against the weak of his Messer as the paired opposite of Duplieren.
records.fullDescription: Begin from a bind reached with a strong Oberhau: strike from your right shoulder powerfully from above so your long edge falls onto his Messer. As he displaces and you feel him go soft, or "weak in the Messer," wind onto his blade toward your left side and drive your arms well high, lifting the hilt and Nagel. From this high winding, hang your point over his Messer from above, carry the arm high over his blade, and let the point sink down the far side into his lower opening, thrusting to an opening below his belt while your edge still controls his steel. You can mirror the whole action from a left-side bind: having bound with the long edge, go high with the arm, remain with that same edge on his Messer, wind over to his left side, and thrust to the opening beyond. The element lives entirely in the winding and hanging of the point across his blade, so keep the arm raised and the point heavy while your strength stays gathered in the hilt and the point does the finishing work below.
records.briefApplication: Choose Mutieren when you feel the opponent go soft in the bind, converting your upper bind into a thrust that drops beneath his blade into his lower opening.
records.fullApplication: Choose Mutieren when you feel the opponent go soft in the bind, converting your upper bind into a thrust that drops beneath his blade into his lower opening. It is the lower-line partner to Duplieren: read the bind Indes, and where Duplieren answers a hard, strong bind by doubling behind his blade above, Mutieren answers a weak, yielding one by winding over and thrusting below, so between the two you can break all four openings from any stroke. Reach it most naturally from a strong Oberhau that he displaces softly, but you can also fold it in after other work: when he catches your cut in the hanging point, wind Indes with the mutating onto his Messer and thrust to his chest or face, or use that same winding to seize his hilt and go into Messernehmen. Be aware it is well answered. An alert opponent can Zucken, twitching his point free the instant you start over his blade, then wind into the hanging point and thrust to your face. He may also meet your mutation by winding his own hanging point against you — right edge high if you come to his right side, to the nearest opening if you come to his left — and once he has deflected you there he can hurry Indes with the long point into your face. So commit only when you truly feel him weak, keep your point controlling his steel as you wind over, and be ready to change your line the moment his point comes alive.

records.briefDescription: Durchlaufen, the eighth element, is Lecküchner's wrestling at the Messer: against an opponent who rushes in high and strong, you close hard, drop the Messer, and run through his arms to grapple, throw, or break.
records.fullDescription: Durchlaufen begins the moment the bind collapses into a clinch. As the opponent drives in with an upper stroke, high with the arms and eager to shove you over, strike the Entrüsthau together with him and close hard, so your hands touch surely on each other. Now, Indes, drop your Messer and grapple. With your left hand grab behind his right elbow on the outside and push him to his left side; simultaneously reach with your right hand or arm behind his right knee-bending, lift the leg, and throw him in front of you. If instead you both bind arm to arm, seize his right hand with your left, raise it high, run your head through beneath his arm, lay it across your shoulder, and rise with your neck and shoulders to break it. When you enter with the Entrüsthau, hold the thumb below on the flat so the blunt short edge strikes his head, then pull firmly with the hilt to draw the hands together before letting the Messer fall to wrestle at close quarters.
records.briefApplication: Choose Durchlaufen against an opponent who rushes in eagerly, high with the arms, and tries to overpower you with force once the bind becomes a clinch.
records.fullApplication: Choose Durchlaufen against an opponent who rushes in eagerly, high with the arms, and tries to overpower you with force once the bind becomes a clinch. It answers exactly the fighter who abandons clean fencing to shove and press, turning his committed rush into a throw. Enter it Indes off the Entrüsthau, feeling whether he is soft or hard in the bind; the master lists running through among the works of Indes, alongside Duplieren, Mutieren, and taking over. Once you own the clinch you flow freely between plays: throw him over the hip or leg, run the head through to break the arm over your shoulder, or, when disarming serves better, pass into Messer Nehmen by seizing his wrist and winding the Messer from his hand, or into Abschneiden by slicing the sharp edge into his wrist. The characteristic finish is to take the balance at his elbow and throw. Beware that it can be countered: if he grabs your right hand and moves to take the balance at your elbow, drop the elbow hard down to your right side against your body and flick the short edge onto his head, or counter-grab his right hand and turn his own throw back upon him. Do not linger in the grips, commit fully, or you hand him the very holds you sought.

records.briefDescription: The tenth element: a close wrestling play where you fold your hilt over his Messer, pull back so your weak drops onto his hand, then fall with both hands onto both Messers and press down to trap his weapon hand.
records.fullDescription: You reach this element from a bind where you have already gone over the top: coming from your right with an Entrüsthau to his left side, bring your hilt above his Messer on his right side so his blade sits trapped beneath yours. From here, pull your hilt backwards along his Messer so the weak of your blade, the point-half, draws down onto his right hand. Indes, fall with your left hand onto both Messers and let your armed right hand drop from above onto both blades as well, so his hand is caught beneath the two weapons between your hands. Press firmly straight down with both hands, pinning his hand under the blades so he cannot lift or free it; because you fall from above, sink your weight through the press rather than muscling with the arms alone, and stay close through his body. Then turn your left side in toward his right and finish freely, for you have grabbed and locked the hand and can throw, disarm, or strike as you please.
records.briefApplication: Choose Hände Drücken when you have folded your hilt over his Messer and want to shut the fight down by trapping his weapon hand rather than trading further cuts.
records.fullApplication: Choose Hände Drücken when you have folded your hilt over his Messer and want to shut the fight down by trapping his weapon hand rather than trading further cuts. It belongs to the family of over-the-hilt plays reached from the Entrüsthau, and it sits close to Abschneiden: where the four cuts slice into the arms, here you pin his hand under both blades and press with both of yours. Use it Indes, the instant your over-grip and backward pull have drawn your weak down onto his hand; the two-handed fall must land while he is still committed to the bind, before he can lift or wind free. Once the press is set and you turn your left side to his right, you own his Messer and can flow into whatever the moment offers: press on into Messer Nehmen to strip his weapon with the empty hand, step behind his foot to throw, or simply cut. Because the technique commits your left hand to the blades, it is a close-play answer inside the bind, not the Zufechten, so do not reach for it at distance. He can unmake it before you set it: feeling the over-grip come, he can wind his own long edge over your hand and cut down first to beat you to it, Zucken his Messer free before your left hand falls, or set your follow-up aside with the empty hand and race you to his own disarm. The whole thing lives in the tempo of the fall; press late and he slips the hand, press in the moment and he is locked.

records.briefDescription: The thirteenth element: passing your Messer and point through the gap between you and the opponent, off a feinted Oberhau, to find strokes, thrusts, and cuts at close or far distance, or to enter wrestling and disarms.
records.fullDescription: Come together in the Zufechten and strike an upper stroke (Oberhau) from your right shoulder straight toward his left side. Indes, before the stroke lands, wind the short (blunt) edge against his Messer and let your point sink. Now carry that lowered point through the space between him and you, passing your Messer across to his right side, and either strike to his head or thrust from above at his face, turning the Messer so the short edge is below. The whole action lives on the feint: the threatened stroke brings his Messer up to meet you, and you wind your blunt edge against it and slip the point under and through rather than completing the blow. It works whether you stand close or far, and you may finish with the point, with strokes, or with cuts. To recover and renew the attack, drive the Messer high above your head with the thumb below on the flat, the point trailing back and the hilt toward the man, then fall from above to his head once more.
records.briefApplication: Reach for it in the Zufechten to deceive a defender with a feinted Oberhau, slipping your point through to strike or thrust at the opening he leaves uncovered.
records.fullApplication: Reach for it in the Zufechten to deceive a defender with a feinted Oberhau, slipping your point through to strike or thrust at the opening he leaves uncovered. Choose Durchgehen against a fencer who brings his Messer up to meet your upper stroke: winding the short edge and dropping the point takes you beneath his blade instead of meeting it, so you arrive on his right side. Once your point is through, work Indes, feeling whether he is soft or hard, and chain freely: twitch through with Zucken to thrust at the other cheek, stab through both cheeks in succession, work Duplieren behind his blade, cut into his arm, or drop to the lower openings. It is also named as your break against his taking-over in the hanging point, going through to remain uninjured, and going through low is the doorway to wrestling and Messer-taking, passing under to seize his hilt or hand. Heed the master's warning that going through in the Messer is done differently than in the sword. Take care, too, that a wary opponent can break it by winding against your Messer and driving his own point to your face so that yours is set off, so keep the point threatening and be ready to wind against him.

records.briefDescription: The fifteenth main element and a disarm ("take the defence"): in the bind you seize his hilt or hand, then twist or press his Messer downward to strip it clean out of his grip and strike through his head.
records.fullDescription: You reach the Messer-taking out of the bind, best after driving in firmly with the Entrüsthau to his left side. As the Messers spark together, do not linger on the blade: carry your hilt high and over his Messer to his right side, laying the crosspiece to the inside of his right elbow, and push firmly from you so his weapon is pinned across. In the same instant fall with your left hand into his bind behind his right hand and pull firmly toward you; his Messer strips free, and you strike through his head. To take with the armed hand instead, catch his stroke between both hands set on your own blade, drive your hilt high on the inside, then fold it from above down over his hand to the wrist joint on the outside and pull firmly to your right side, stepping your rear foot back for weight. You may also take purely with the empty hand: as he strikes, bow under his Messer, leap to his right side, and press your left arm between his hand and hilt to lever the weapon loose. Whichever mode you use, remember the master's rule: always fall to the weak of his Messer with your right hand, winding over to his left and pressing rapidly downward.
records.briefApplication: Reach for Messer nehmen in the bind, Indes, when you feel his hilt or hand exposed after a displacement — to end it by stripping his weapon rather than trading cuts.
records.fullApplication: Reach for Messer nehmen in the bind, Indes, when you feel his hilt or hand exposed after a displacement — to end it by stripping his weapon rather than trading cuts. It belongs to close play: choose it when you have bound firmly (as after an Entrüsthau) and feel him committed, so that levering his cross or wrist is surer than doubling or mutating against his blade. It also flows out of the hanging point and out of taking over, where you fall with the empty hand onto his hilt and simply pull downward. Expect him to defend, for the master gives breaks against every taking. If, as you press down to strip him, he falls with both hands onto his own hilt and pulls firmly down, he reclaims the Messer and strikes through your head — the counter the master names "freely unbridled," and the same break answers the other takings. He may instead wind his Messer around so the short edge is below, go high with the hilt, and set the point to your chest, or seize your gripping arm and lever it back against you. Guard against these by keeping your point online as you disarm and stepping well offline, so that if the strip fails you can still wind to the langer Ort or strike anew rather than be left grasping empty-handed.

records.briefDescription: Zufechten is the onset, the approach phase before the bind, in which you close the distance and drive a decisive stroke to the openings to seize the initiative rather than standing still and waiting for the attack.
records.fullDescription: As you come toward the man, do not stand frozen with the Messer and wait for his strokes; carry it in a ready guard, most often Luginsland with the arm stretched high and the long edge forward, or chambered on your right shoulder or in the Schrankhut at the right leg with the left foot forward. Keep your attention on his four peaks, the openings, not on his blade, and hold your displacement before your head as a shield. When the measure closes, leap with the right foot well out to the side and unwind the body into a master strike, whether a Zornhau from the shoulder, a Wecker with the right edge, or an Entrüsthau to the upper peak, leading with the long or short edge and driving the point online. Indes, as the edges spark together, wind the point into his face and thrust to the nearest opening. The whole phase is forward, brave motion: stay light on the feet, strike sooner than he does, and let the guard flow straight into the stroke without pausing to see what he will do.
records.briefApplication: Use the Zufechten to win the Vor: close bravely and strike first to the openings so your opponent is forced to displace and answer you rather than the reverse.
records.fullApplication: Use the Zufechten to win the Vor: close bravely and strike first to the openings so your opponent is forced to displace and answer you rather than the reverse. This is the phase that decides who leads, and the master warns that whoever only wants to displace will be beaten by the whole art, so never stand and merely wait for his strokes. Read his guard as you approach and choose the strike that breaks it: meet Luginsland with the Entrüsthau, break the Stier or Eber with the Wecker, and answer a low attack by overrunning from above. Aim at the four peaks, not at his Messer, and keep your head covered as you go. If he commits a stroke or only raises his Messer to strike around, chase it: fall in with the point and thrust to the nearest opening before he recovers, as in Nachreisen. Should he reach the Vor sooner than you, leap offline and set his cut aside with Absetzen or displace, then take the Vor back with your Nach by working Indes in the bind, winding the point to his face, changing through below with Durchwechseln if he presses to the blade, or twitching off to strike another peak. The onset is countered only by a man who wins the Vor first or steps clean out of your line, so hold the measure, keep moving, and let your guard become the stroke.

records.briefDescription: Krieg is the close-quarters winding phase that opens the instant your blades bind, the flurry of windings, thrusts, doublings and slices decided by feeling and Indes, as opposed to the Zufechten of the onset.
records.fullDescription: The Krieg is not a single strike but the whole close play you conduct once one Messer touches the other. Lecküchner defines it as the four windings and the work you draw from them with the point into the four openings. Enter it straight from a bind, for instance after a Zornhau that he displaces: go high with the arm so the hilt rides up before your head and the point hangs down, then wind the point over his Messer from above to the opening. Keep the long edge on his blade as you turn the hand; if you wind to his left, thrust to the face on that side, and if he sets the thrust aside, go high again to the other peak, under his right arm to his chest. Throughout, read whether he is soft or hard on the Messer and let that feeling, not your eyes, choose the winding. Always keep the arm high and the point sunk toward the openings, so that each turn threatens with point, long edge, or short edge at once, and follow him from one peak to the next whenever he displaces.
records.briefApplication: Choose the Krieg the moment a bind forms, working Indes off the feeling of his blade to strike, thrust, or slice into whichever of the four openings he leaves.
records.fullApplication: Choose the Krieg the moment a bind forms, working Indes off the feeling of his blade to strike, thrust, or slice into whichever of the four openings he leaves. It is the answer to the master's warning that whoever only displaces will be hurt by the whole art: rather than parry and reset, you stay on his Messer and pursue the next peak. If he is hard in the bind and shoves against your strong, double with Duplieren, going high with the arm to strike behind his blade with the short edge; if he is soft or gives at the weak, mutate below with Mutieren, sinking the upper bind into a thrust to his lower opening. When he presses in or runs high with the arm, fall on it with the Schnitt; when he chases your winding, twitch off with Zucken and thrust to a fresh opening. Your own windings are answered in kind, for he may drop under your point with Durchwechseln or wind against you to steal the line, so feel constantly and keep the hanging point covering your head as you work. Driven rightly, the Krieg lets him hardly come away unstruck; you shame him above and below, sinking the point onto opening after opening until he can neither defend nor strike back.

records.briefDescription: The four openings are the opponent's target quarters — upper and lower, split at the belt, right and left of the centreline — that you strike toward instead of aiming at his Messer itself.
records.fullDescription: Picture the opponent divided into four quarters: the belt separates the upper openings from the lower, and his centreline separates his right from his left, giving an upper-right, upper-left, lower-right, and lower-left target — Lecküchner also names these the four peaks. From the Zufechten you keep all four in mind and, crucially, do not strike at his Messer; you drive your stroke, thrust, or point at whichever quarter stands bare. The openings are equally where the war — the windings — does its work: in the bind you wind the point over or under his Messer and shoot it from one quarter to the next, over his blade to the face on his left side, then high to the other peak under his right arm to the chest. Break the upper openings by doubling against the strong of his Messer and the lower ones by mutating against the weak. Whether you lead with the point, the long edge, or the short edge, your work is always aimed against an opening and never against his steel.
records.briefApplication: Use the four openings as your targeting map: from the onset strike boldly at whichever quarter stands uncovered rather than hammering at his Messer.
records.fullApplication: Use the four openings as your targeting map: from the onset strike boldly at whichever quarter stands uncovered rather than hammering at his Messer. This principle underlies every attack — when you throw a Zornhau, a Wecker, or an Entrüsthau, you aim it at a specific opening, and it turns his defence into a trap, because he can guard only one quarter at a time, so covering one peak bares another. When he displaces, do not stall; strike Indes to the next opening, from one peak to the other, exactly as each Entrüsthau is driven to a fresh peak — from an upper peak to the lower, and across to the far side. In the bind, feel whether he is soft or hard: read the opening he leaves and work the war, winding the point to the face above or the chest below. If he binds strong and high, double against the strong into the upper opening; if he binds weak, mutate against the weak into the lower. If he holds his point online against your opening, do not change through — remain and work; but if he lets his point drift wide, change through to the far quarter. The same concept drives setting-on and drawing-after, where you shoot the long point to the nearest open quarter as he recovers or withdraws. Keep your own four quarters covered — hold your shield, the displacement, in front of your head — even as you hunt his.

records.briefDescription: The Vier Leger are the Messer's four principal wards — Bastei, Luginsland, Stier, and Eber — the standing positions from which you defend, threaten, and launch your strokes, each broken by its own displacement.
records.fullDescription: The four guards are your resting and threatening positions throughout the system, and each has a fixed form. In Bastei, the bulwark, put your left foot forward and hold the Messer with a stretched arm before you, the point resting on the ground and the short edge uppermost. In Luginsland, the watchtower, again lead with the left foot and stretch the arm high in front of your head with the long, sharp edge turned against the man so the point looms overhead. Stier, the bull, is a high side ward: left foot forward, hilt held before your head on the right so the short edge faces you and the point menaces his face from above. Eber, the boar, is its low counterpart: left foot forward, Messer at the right leg with the hilt at your hip, the short blunt edge above and the point angled up toward his face like a tusk; you may also form it on the left, hilt lowered and long edge turned up. From every ward the long point is your surest defense, so keep your arm and balance settled and let the point threaten, rather than displacing for its own sake.
records.briefApplication: Choose your ward to shape the exchange: each guard defends a line and threatens an opening, and each is broken by one particular master strike.
records.fullApplication: Choose your ward to shape the exchange: each guard defends a line and threatens an opening, and each is broken by one particular master strike. The high Luginsland is undone by the Entrüsthau, which strips away everything struck from above; the low Bastei is opened by the Geferhau; the high Stier is broken by the Wecker, stepping offline to wind the point into his face; and the low Eber is forced by the Zwinger. So read the ward he stands in and reply with its counter — though the master teaches that the long point is often surer still, for the guards cannot protect themselves against it: go high and thrust it at his face to break a Stier, or sink the Messer low and drive the ready point up to break an Eber, catching him before his own stroke lands. Do not simply displace and wait: whoever only parries is hurt by the whole art. Stand in the guard, seize the Vor, and if he binds or presses, work Indes out of it — wind into the Stier from the hangings, change through beneath his blade when he reaches for the bind, or set on and draw after as he recovers. From Bastei especially you can catch a man who runs in on your forward point, then change through to his next opening.

records.briefDescription: Lecküchner's name for his six master strikes — the Zornhau, Wecker, Entrüsthau, Zwinger, Geferhau, and Wincker — the core offensive system whose true working stays hidden from the untrained eye.
records.fullDescription: These six strokes are the striking heart of Lecküchner's Messer, standing roughly where Liechtenauer's master hews stand in the longsword, and most share a common delivery. Set your left foot forward and chamber the Messer on your right shoulder or in the Schranckhut, its point toward the ground and the blunt short edge turned to the man. As the opponent commits, leap offline with your striking foot and drive the cut firmly onto his Messer, most often with the long edge, though several turn the short edge to the head. Do not let the stroke end at the cut: the instant the blades spark together, wind the point up into his face so the long edge rides above. Each of the six is aimed to break a particular guard or attack, and their name is earned here — the visible cut is only the doorway, while the true work stays concealed in the windings, thrusts, and edge-changes that spring from it once you feel the bind. Carry the blade with your stepping body behind the Nagel, not the arm alone.
records.briefApplication: Use the Verborgene Häue as your primary offense in the Zufechten, choosing the one stroke that breaks the opponent's guard and lets you seize the Vor.
records.fullApplication: Use the Verborgene Häue as your primary offense in the Zufechten, choosing the one stroke that breaks the opponent's guard and lets you seize the Vor. Match the strike to what stands before you: the Zornhau answers any stroke from above, the Wecker breaks the Stier and the Eber, the Entrüsthau undoes the Luginsland and descending cuts, the Zwinger constrains a downward blow, the Geferhau feints high and shows the changing-through, and the Wincker punishes free-fighters who parry openly. Their power is never in the cut alone: because whoever only displaces will be hurt by the whole art, do not halt once you bind. Feel Indes whether he is soft or hard, then flow to the nearest opening — wind the point to his face, use Durchwechseln if he chases your blade, Duplieren against the strong of his Messer or Mutieren against the weak, or Zucken to twitch off and strike anew. It is from these six that Lecküchner's many elements grow, so treat each less as a single blow than as the entrance to the war, and let foot, edge, and point keep working until the opening is yours.

records.briefDescription: The four master strikes that break the four guards, one matched to each Leger, where displacing means striking aggressively through a guard to cover and threaten in a single tempo rather than passively parrying.
records.fullDescription: There is no single posture here; the Vier Versetzen are four named master strikes, each assigned to break one of the four guards: the Wecker breaks the Stier, the Entrüsthau breaks the Luginsland, the Zwinger breaks the Eber, and the Geférhau breaks the Bastei. Whichever you throw, the mechanics are shared. From the Zufechten, set your left foot forward with the Messer chambered on the right shoulder, in the Schranckhut at the leg, or high in the Luginsland, and as the opening shows, leap offline with your right foot toward his side. Drive the matched strike long from a stretched arm so that its blade stays as a shield before your head, cutting through his guard rather than beside it, and immediately wind the point into his face. The leading edge follows the stroke: the long edge for the Wecker and Geférhau, the short blunt edge laid long over his Messer for the Zwinger, and the strong of the blade behind the Entrüsthau. Footwork carries the blow, so step well to the side with every strike, letting the cut lengthen and land from a safe line.
records.briefApplication: Use the Vier Versetzen in the Zufechten to break a man who waits in a static guard, seizing the Vor by striking through his Leger instead of standing back to parry.
records.fullApplication: Use the Vier Versetzen in the Zufechten to break a man who waits in a static guard, seizing the Vor by striking through his Leger instead of standing back to parry. This is the master's answer to his own warning that a man who only displaces will be shamed and beaten: you do not wait to ward his blow, you displace his guard with a stroke that covers and threatens at once. Read which Leger he holds and throw its counter, the Wecker against the Stier, the Entrüsthau against the Luginsland and any descending stroke, the Zwinger against the Eber, the Geférhau against the Bastei. As your blade arrives, work Indes and wind the point to his face into a Langer Ort so he can do nothing; if he answers, flow on. Should he displace hard, double behind his blade with Duplieren or mutate to the lower opening with Mutieren; should he chase your Messer with his parry, change through below with Durchwechseln and thrust to the far side; should he bind firmly, twitch off with Zucken to another peak. Beware the same weapon turned on you, for a man who shoots the Langer Ort first can break your incoming strike, and one who displaces freely or crookedly invites the Wincker, so keep your shield, the displacement itself, well before your head and never merely parry in return.

records.briefDescription: The rhymed mnemonic verse that epitomizes Lecküchner's whole Messer art in terse couplets, closely modeled on Liechtenauer's, which the master then quotes and glosses element by element.
records.fullDescription: Treat the Zettel as the skeleton on which every technique hangs: a sequence of terse rhymed couplets meant to be memorized whole, then fleshed out by the master's prose gloss. Its foreword sets the mindset, warning that whoever only displaces will be hurt by the entire art, and fixes the timing words Vor, Nach and Indes as the keep of the whole art, alongside reading the weak and strong of the blade. It then tells you how to carry yourself: fence one-handed, the free hand laid on your back, bringing it to your chest only when you mean to wrestle or take the Messer. From there the verse names the six hidden strokes in order — Zornhau, Wecker, Entrüsthau, Zwinger, Geferhau and Wincker — then the seventeen further elements, opening with the four guards (Bastei, Luginsland, Stier, Eber) and running on through displacing, drawing after, overrunning, changing through, twitching, the four cuts, the bow, the hangings and winding against the openings, twenty-three main elements in all.
records.briefApplication: Recite the Zettel to hold the entire art in memory and to locate any play, since its verses tell you which stroke or element answers a given guard or bind.
records.fullApplication: Recite the Zettel to hold the entire art in memory and to locate any play, since its verses tell you which stroke or element answers a given guard or bind. Because each couplet is a heading, the Recital doubles as an index: when an opponent settles into Luginsland you recall the line pairing the Entrüsthau against it; when he takes the Stier or Eber you reach for the Wecker; when he binds hard you find Zucken (twitching) and Winden (winding) further down the list. The gloss layers breakings and counter-breakings onto each verse, so a single line grows into a chain — strike, displace, then work Indes into Durchwechseln (changing through), Duplieren, or the four cuts as his reaction dictates. Learn it in order, for the master builds later elements on earlier ones: the six strokes come first because many good elements come from them, and the seventeen that follow — displacing, drawing after, overrunning, running through, the bow, taking the Messer, the hangings and winding — assume you already own the strokes. The Recital is never itself thrown or parried; it is the map, and every other Messer element is one point charted on it.
